strict_queue_context.vignette:
A man in his 80s was brought to the emergency department after a cardiac arrest. According to paramedics, the patient was last seen healthy by his family 4 hours earlier, then was found unresponsive and pulseless in the bathroom. He underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, receiving 4 doses of epinephrine intravenously and endotracheal tube intubation with return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 10 minutes. Family later revealed he had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and had been complaining of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation. A family member witnessed him struggling for air before losing consciousness.

Initial rhythm was pulseless electrical activity.

- ECG findings:    - Sinus rhythm at approximately 100 beats per minute    - Right axis deviation    - Prolonged QRS duration with rsR' complexes in lead V1    - Wide S waves in leads I and V6    - Prolonged r to peak R' time in lead V1    - QT interval of 360 ms measurable in leads V4-V6    - QRS duration of 133 ms in inferior leads  - Coronary angiography:    No acute occlusions found  Image Title: Figure 1. 12-Lead Electrocardiogram at Presentation  Image Title: Figure 2. Inferior and Lateral Leads From Repeated Electrocardiogram Demonstrating Discernible T Waves  Image Title: Figure 3. Leads II, III, V5, and V6 of Initial Electrocardiogram

A 55-year-old white woman with a history of diverticulosis and colonic polyps presented with new-onset flulike symptoms followed by low-grade fever, facial crusted plaques, and 4 weeks of bloody and watery diarrhea. Her facial lesions initially presented as ill-defined pink patches over her cheeks and red papules on her forehead. Over the next 4 days, the lesions spread to her chest, abdomen, back, and left buttock, and a single papule appeared on the right lower extremity. Her low-grade fevers and diarrhea persisted throughout this 4-day period.

In the emergency department, she was febrile and tachycardic. Physical findings included:- 6 × 7-cm well-demarcated vegetative crusted plaques on the bilateral cheeks- Several discrete, round, 1- to 2-cm crusted plaques on the temple- Discrete pustules, vesicles, and umbilicated papules on cheeks and temple- Lesions on chest, abdomen, back, and left buttock- Painful subcutaneous nodules over lower extremities- Polyarthralgia

Laboratory Tests:- Mild leukocytosis with normal differential- Mildly elevated transaminase and alkaline phosphatase levels- Negative wound culture- Blood cultures showed no growth- Negative PCR for herpes simplex virus- Negative direct fluorescent antibody assay for varicella-zoster virusPathology:- Forehead lesion biopsy: Intradermal neutrophilic inflammation with ulceration and intracorneal neutrophils. Special stains negative for microorganisms- Right thigh biopsy: Septal panniculitis with Miescher radial granulomas- Colonoscopy: Moderate inflammation, edema, erosions, and pseudopolyps in the sigmoid colonImages:Image 1 Title: Clinical Appearance of Facial Neutrophilic DermatosisImage 1 Description: A, A 6 × 7-cm, well-demarcated, vegetative crusted plaque on the left cheek and a discrete, round, 1- to 2-cm crusted plaque on the foreheadImage 2 Title: Histopathological Findings of Facial Neutrophilic DermatosisImage 2 Description: Shave biopsy specimen from forehead lesion showing diffuse intradermal neutrophilic infiltrate with central ulceration

A man in his 20s presented with complaints of intermittent palpitations for 2 days, which had worsened in the previous hour. He had no history of chest pain, dyspnea, congestion, or fever. There was no past cardiac history or family history of similar complaints.

Blood pressure was 110/72 mm Hg, respiratory rate was 14 bpm. Cardiovascular system examination results were unremarkable.

- ECG Studies:    Image A Title: Initial ECG    Image A Description: Wide complex tachycardia at rate of 190 bpm with atypical left bundle branch morphology (QS in leads V1-V5 with transition in V6), QRS duration of 146 ms with no evidence of AV dissociation, and inferior axis.        Image B Title: Post-treatment ECG    Image B Description: Normal sinus rhythm at 64 bpm with normal QRS axis. Precordial T-wave inversion in leads V1 to V5, I, and aVL. Epsilon wave present in lead V4 and low voltage in limb leads.  - Echocardiography:    Global hypokinesia of right ventricle, dilated RV, ballooned out RVOT measuring 35 mm with tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion of 17 mm.      - Cardiac MRI:    Findings: Grossly dilated RV, high RV end diastolic volume of 219.9 mL, RVOT diameter of 31 mm, RV ejection fraction of 19.3%. Postcontrast hyperenhancement along RV free wall, RVOT apical wall, RV aspect of septum, and in basal inferior, midcavity inferior, and inferoseptal myocardium of left ventricle.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 30-year-old woman presented with a large unhealed ulcer measuring 20 × 14-cm² that had persisted for the past 3 years. The patient had a patch of healthy skin (7.5 × 4 cm²) on her left forearm. Blood cell genotyping revealed compound heterozygous alterations (c.2992 + 2T>G and c.8621-30A>G) at splice sites in COL7A1.

The patient presented with:- A 20 × 14-cm² persistent ulcer on the back- A patch of healthy skin (7.5 × 4 cm²) on the left forearm, lacking blistering

1. Genetic Testing:- Blood cell genotyping showed compound heterozygous alterations in COL7A1- RNA transcript analysis using MinION platform:  * Affected skin epidermis: Dominant RNA transcripts with premature stop codons, wild-type reads rare (1.1%)  * Potentially revertant area epidermis: High rates of wild-type transcripts (35.0%)  * Revertant skin dermis: Wild-type reads rare (1.9%)2. strict_queue_context.vignette:
A woman in her 60s presented with an itchy plaque on the mid-back. She had had a lesion at that site since childhood, which had remained asymptomatic and pea sized for most of that time. However, over the 10 years prior to presentation it had gradually increased in size and became itchy. There was also occasional oozing of serosanguineous fluid and bleeding from the lesion.

Examination revealed a 1.5 × 1.0-cm well-defined erythematous plaque with overlying ulceration on the mid-back, 1 cm left of the spine. Adjoining skin showed a horseshoe-shaped oval area of lichenification.

- Histopathological examination:    - Revealed a circumscribed tumor contiguous with adjoining normal epidermis and delineated from underlying dermis by continuous apocrine epithelial lining    - Tumor epithelium with multiple papillary projections with vascular, plasma cell–rich stroma    - Several foci showed papillary projections lined by multilayered epithelium with atypical cells, few mitotic figures, and areas of necrosis but no dermal invasion      - Immunohistochemical analysis:    - p63 staining positive in myoepithelial cell layers    - Adjacent skin showed dermal papillae with congophilic amorphous eosinophilic deposits    - Pan-cytokeratin (AE1/3) immunostain positive  Images:  Figure 1 Title: Clinical Image of the Patient  Description: A 1.5 × 1.0-cm well-defined erythematous plaque with indented margin and overlying ulceration, located on the mid-back 1 cm left to the spine. Adjoining skin shows a horseshoe-shaped oval area of lichenification.  Figure 2 Title: Histopathologic Findings From Lesional Specimens  Description: Multiple microscopic images showing tumor architecture, cellular details, immunohistochemical staining, and dermal deposits.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A woman in her 40s presented with a 10-year history of progressive skin thickening and subcutaneous enlargement of the right side of her nose and right cheek. She had been seen by several dermatologists and otolaryngologists and had undergone nondiagnostic skin biopsies. She underwent a septorhinoplasty 6 months prior due to collapse of her right nasal ala. During surgery, significant submucosal tissue was noted and removed from the right nasal cavity. She initially improved but noticed enlargement of soft tissue with thickening of the overlying skin on her right cheek and right side of her nose several months later.

Clinical examination revealed slightly hyperplastic soft tissue with dilated patulous follicles involving the right medial malar cheek and right nasal ala in addition to deviation of the nasal tip.

- Surgical Pathology:    1. Initial septorhinoplasty specimens showed fibroadipose tissue and vascular proliferation    2. Initial skin biopsy was interpreted as sebaceous hyperplasia    3. Review of surgical specimens revealed:       - Subcutaneous-based proliferation of spindle cells with varying density       - Thickened and fragmented collagen bundles       - Mature adipocytes extending into skeletal tissue       - Spindle cells had bland cytomorphology with tapered nuclei and ill-defined cytoplasm       - No cellular pleomorphism observed  - Images:    Image Title: Clinical image    Image Description: Shows facial asymmetry with deviation of the nasal tip    Image Title: Hematoxylin-eosin stain    Image Description: Shows interstitial proliferation of spindle cells within mature adipocytes extending between bundles of skeletal muscle    Image Title: Hematoxylin-eosin stain    Image Description: Shows mature adipocytes separated by proliferation of spindle cells associated with fragments of thickened collagen

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A white man in his 30s with a 7-year history of severe, mechanical, low back pain and long-standing mental depression. Current medications include duloxetine hydrochloride, clonazepam, oxcarbazepine, fentanyl, sulpiride, zopiclone, omeprazole magnesium, and baclofen. Patient admitted to self-administering subcutaneous injections of meperidine, 100 mg 4 times per day, for the past 3 years, at different sites, including the deltoid areas and abdomen.

Large and deep, irregularly shaped, cutaneous ulcer on the dorsum of right forearm with necrotic tissue and muscle exposure at the base. Woody induration of skin on both forearms and abdominal region. Bilateral contracture of deltoid, triceps, and biceps muscles. Active and passive range of motion restricted at shoulders and elbows. No signs of joint inflammation.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Elevated serum creatinine kinase (192 U/L; reference range, 0-174 U/L)
  - Normal complete blood cell count
  - Normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate
  - Normal antinuclear antibody
  - Normal rheumatoid factor
  - Normal aspartate aminotransferase
  - Normal alanine aminotransaminase
  - Normal aldolase levels
  - Normal serum electrophoresis
  - Negative culture specimens for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungal organisms

- Histopathology:
  Image Title: Wedge biopsy from indurated skin of abdominal region
  Image Description: Shows lobular panniculitis, subcutaneous fat lobules with necrotic adipocytes and dense inflammatory infiltrates composed mainly of foamy histiocytes. Severe fibrosis in deep dermis and subcutaneous septa. Foreign-body giant cells and macrophages with large, foamy cytoplasm present. No evidence of thrombosis or vasculitis. No polarizable foreign material identified.

- Muscle Biopsy:
  Deltoid muscle biopsy showed no muscle involvement

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with new and progressive satellite lesions while undergoing pembrolizumab therapy. Two years earlier, he had undergone a wide local excision with graft repair for a left posterior auricular scalp lesion. An incidentally resected lymph node was found to be focally involved, with no evidence of distant metastatic disease. Within months, multiple unresectable satellite lesions appeared. He received 4 cycles of ipilimumab, followed by a second wide local excision when new lesions appeared. Additional satellite lesions developed and he began pembrolizumab therapy, but after 5 cycles, local progression occurred in the satellite lesions.

Multiple satellite lesions were present on the left posterior auricular scalp area. After treatment, clinically regressed lesions with persistent black pigmentation were noted.

Title: Recurrent Melanoma Lesions on the Left Posterior Auricular Scalp Before and After T-VEC Therapy    Figure 2. Title: Histopathologic Findings of T-VEC–Treated Melanoma Lesions    Description: Shows complete tumor regression and neutrophil-rich mixed inflammation; MART-1 immunostain confirms complete tumor regression

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 61-year-old woman with cirrhosis secondary to alcohol use disorder in remission. Past medical history included esophageal varices, rectal varices, ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and recurrent pleural effusion. Risk factors included a remote history of intranasal cocaine use and multiple tattoos. No history of blood transfusions before 1990, intravenous drug use, or high-risk sexual behavior. Three years after initial evaluation, she developed clinical decompensation requiring multiple paracenteses, thoracenteses, and blood transfusions for gastrointestinal bleeding. Three months into this period of decline, she had a dental extraction.

Patient presented with hepatic encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, and recurrent pleural effusion. Mental status showed acute decline. Progressive deterioration led to increased encephalopathy with concurrent hypotension requiring critical care unit transfer.

- Laboratory Tests:
  * Aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase elevated to greater than 1000 U/L
  * Negative urine drug screen
  * Negative blood cultures
  * Initial negative HCV antibody, later positive
  * HCV viral load: 4,510,319 copies/mL (Hospital Day 4)

- Imaging Studies:
  * Doppler ultrasound scan of liver vasculature performed

- Other Tests:
  * Negative evaluation for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus
  * Negative thoracentesis and paracentesis

- Pathology:
  Title: Liver Explant Histology
  Description: Demonstrated micronodular cirrhosis with dense fibrosis, scattered simple cysts, and bile duct hamartomas

A 34-year-old Thai man with a history of hypertension and tobacco use disorder, and a family history significant for polycythemia, hypertension, and stroke in his father. He initially presented with worsening bifrontal headaches, nausea, vomiting, and right-sided blurry vision. He was not adherent to his antihypertensive regimen. Three months later, he presented again with right-sided frontal headache, photophobia, tingling in his right fingers, nausea, and vomiting. He reported missing a few doses of his carvedilol and had cut down on his smoking.

Blood pressures in the emergency department ranged from 180 to 190/80-90 mm Hg during initial presentation. On second presentation, systolic blood pressures were 150 to 170 mm Hg. National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score was 2 because of complete left homonymous hemianopsia.

- Laboratory tests: Initial presentation showed hemoglobin 20.2 g/dL, hematocrit 54.8%, MCV 74 fL, and thrombocytopenia (91,000/mm³). Second presentation showed hemoglobin 20.1 g/dL, hematocrit 57.2%, MCV 76 fL, and thrombocytopenia (76,000/mm³). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated (21 mm/h). Erythropoietin was normal (7.8 mIU/mL).- Imaging studies:  - CT Head: Left occipital intraparenchymal hemorrhage with intravascular extension (first presentation)  - CT Head: Right posterior parietal intraparenchymal hemorrhage (4.7 × 2.9 × 4.2 cm) with blood product in the right lateral ventricle and minimal midline shift (second presentation)  - MRI Brain: No underlying masses  - Peripheral smear: Showed microcytosis and thrombocytopenia without toxic granulations or blast cells- Hemoglobin Electrophoresis Results:  Hb A: 0.0%  Hb F: 1.7%  Hb A2: 4.4%  Hb E: 34.0%  Hb Tak: 59.9%

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 63-year-old woman presented with difficult-to-treat hypertension. Medical history included bone and central diabetes insipidus diagnosed via femoral biopsy 12 years ago, and liver involvement three years prior that was treated with cytarabine for one year. The patient had untreated dyslipidemia (LDL cholesterol 3.11 mmol/L). She was not a smoker and did not have diabetes. Her body mass index was 19.22 kg/m². No relevant family history was reported. The patient did not report angina, exertional dyspnea, or claudication.

Blood pressure was 198/106 mmHg without orthostatic hypotension or anisosphygmia, and heart rate was 65 beats/min. The cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable, and a continuous murmur was heard in the epigastric region.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Serum creatinine: 96.36 μmol/L (1.09 mg/dL)    * Potassium: 4.4 mmol/L    * B-type natriuretic peptide: 82,500 pg/mL    * Inflammatory markers: normal    * Urinalysis: unremarkable without albuminuria  - Imaging Studies:    * Transthoracic echocardiogram: left ventricular mass index of 110 g/m² without other relevant changes    * Abdominal CT angiogram:      Title: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT      Description: Right kidney atrophy without discernible right renal artery and high-grade ostial stenosis of the left renal, celiac trunk, and superior mesenteric arteries    * Diethylenetriamine pentaacetate renogram: confirmed right kidney functional exclusion    * Renal vein catheterization: no signs of renin production lateralization

A 71-year-old man presented with three weeks of jaundice, weight loss, abdominal pain, and dark-colored urine. He also reported bilateral lower-extremity weakness that was most noticeable when attempting to arise from a chair, resulting in several ground-level falls. He had no history of autoimmune or neuromuscular conditions. Despite his recent falls, he did not have any prolonged periods of being down that could contribute to muscle injury. He had been taking atorvastatin as a home medication.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 65-year-old man with a history of hepatitis B, hepatitis C, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity presented with several months of facial swelling, dysphagia, and dysarthria. Shortly thereafter, he developed a pruritic rash on his trunk and upper extremities. He did not report a personal or family history of angioedema. His medications included lisinopril, atorvastatin, albuterol, and ibuprofen for rheumatoid arthritis. The patient had discontinued etanercept six months before presentation. He presented to the emergency department two weeks after seeing his primary care provider for a persistent periorbital, chest, and upper extremity rash. His rash worsened, and he noted new throat swelling and weakness.

Vital signs were stable on arrival. Physical examination was notable for anasarca and a diffuse coalescent erythematous rash over the extremities, chest, and abdomen, with scaling and crusting of the back. There was a heliotrope rash and erythematous lip swelling. He had weakness to resistance in all extremities and a muffled voice without tongue swelling. Over several days, the patient's shoulder and hip weakness progressed, and he could not lift his arms above his head or stand without assistance.

- Laboratory Tests:    - Basic metabolic panel and complete blood count were unremarkable    - Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate    - Negative viral respiratory panel    - C4, C1q, and C1 esterase inhibitor were unremarkable    - Normal serum and urine protein electrophoresis    - Elevated transaminases    - Elevated anti-Sjögren syndrome–related antigen A autoantibodies    - High antinuclear antibody titers    - Negative anti-Jo antibody    - Elevated creatine kinase    - Positive myositis panel for anti-SAE antibodies  - Imaging Studies:    - CT neck: Mild submental inflammatory stranding with no discrete fluid collection or abscess    - Liver ultrasound: Hepatic steatosis    - CT chest: Multiple nodular and airspace opacities, including right lower lobe nodule  - Pathology:    - Skin biopsy results were consistent with Wong-type presentation

A 52-year-old woman presented with a mass on her left parotid gland causing otalgia. She did not report any constitutional symptoms initially. Eighteen months after initial presentation, the patient developed facial swelling, abdominal bloating, easy bruising, 30-lb weight gain. Past medical history was unremarkable.

Initial examination: Blood pressure was 120/78 mm Hg, normal. Later examination (18 months): Blood pressure elevated to 193/113 mm Hg. Physical findings included facial swelling, abdominal bloating, easy bruising, and significant weight gain (30 lbs).

- Initial Imaging: Head, neck, and chest imaging showed a 2.4-cm parotid mass and a 2.7-cm level IIB lymph node.- Fine-needle aspiration biopsy: Showed features of a salivary gland neoplasm with atypia.- Laboratory Tests (18 months after presentation):  * Serum cortisol: 1151 nmol/L (normal range: 133-537)  * ACTH level: 78.5 pmol/L (normal range: 1.6-13.9)  * Random blood glucose: 16 mmol/L (elevated)  * Potassium: 3.0 mmol/L (normal range: 3.5-5.0)  * Aspartate aminotransferase: 62 IU/L (normal: <33)  * Alanine aminotransferase: 51 IU/L (normal: <32)  * 24-hour urine cortisol: 1375 mmol/d (normal: <275) on day 1, 1228 mmol/d on day 2  * Midnight salivary cortisol: 68.6 and 59.7 nmol/L (normal: <11.3) on two consecutive nights- Histological Examination: Stage T2N2B, with metastases in 5 of 47 lymph nodes, lymphovascular and perineural invasion- Immunohistochemical staining: Positive for ACTH in 30-40% of invasive tumor cells; negative for synaptophysin and chromogranin

Initial contrast-enhanced CT:- Revealed hepatosplenomegaly- Contrast-enhanced defective area in kidney2. Coronary angiography:- Total occlusion of atrioventricular branch of right coronary artery- 90% stenotic lesions with >3 mm coronary ectasia in left circumflex artery3. Optical coherence tomography:- Showed blurring of intravascular structure- Intimal thickening- Medial vessel destruction- Thrombi in RCA and LCx lesions4. Follow-up contrast-enhanced CT:- New intrahepatic arterial luminal irregularities- Enlarged contrast-enhanced defective area in kidneySARS-CoV-2 PCR test results were repeatedly negative

strict_queue_context.reference_diagnosis: CD5+ Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma presenting as Cavernous Sinus Syndrome
strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a medical history of atrial fibrillation, sick sinus syndrome with pacemaker placement, prostate cancer treated with radiation and hormonal therapy, obstructive sleep apnea, left-sided Bell's palsy, and tobacco misuse presented with 3 weeks of right-sided temporal headache and 3 days of diplopia.

Physical examination revealed:- Preexisting left-sided incomplete facial nerve palsy- Right cranial nerve VI and III palsies- Visual acuity and peripheral vision intact bilaterally- No miosis, mydriasis, conjunctival injection, or lacrimation- Severe photosensitivity- Normal funduscopic examination- No other neurologic deficits

Laboratory Tests:- Initial complete blood count: unremarkable- Comprehensive metabolic panel: unremarkable- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: unremarkable- C-reactive protein: unremarkable- Thyroid-stimulating hormone: unremarkable- CSF microbiology: negative- CSF cytology: no malignant cellsImaging Studies:1. CTA of head and neck:   - Air fluid levels in bilateral sphenoid and maxillary sinuses   - Otherwise unremarkable2. MRI of brain and orbits with/without contrast:   Image Title: Axial and coronal T1 MRI with contrast pretreatment   Image Description: Avid irregular enhancement within the right cavernous sinus and enlargement of the right side compared with the left3. CT thorax findings:   - Left pleural effusion   - Mediastinal lymphadenopathy   - Mass-like thickening of the posterior left pleura4. CT abdomen and pelvis:   - Mesenteric lymphadenopathyPathology:- Biopsy of posterior left pleural thickening showed CD5+, CD10−, non-germinal center B-cell type- Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis: negative for Myc, BCL6, t(14;18)/IGH-BCL2, and t(11;14)/CCND1-IGH gene rearrangements- Bone marrow biopsy: normal

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 33-year-old man with no medical history presented with a 1-day history of hemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and dyspnea on exertion. He did not report orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, sore throat, runny nose, diarrhea, urinary symptoms, night sweats, or recent tuberculosis contact. He had received the Johnson & Johnson COVID vaccination approximately 4 weeks before presentation.

Initial vitals:- Temperature: 98.9 °F- Heart rate: 76 beats/min- Blood pressure: 90/55 mm Hg- SpO₂: 99% on room airPhysical examination showed a lethargic man with unremarkable cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations. Head and neck examination showed no lymphadenopathy. He developed a low-grade fever of 100 °F on day 1.

Laboratory Tests:- Elevated inflammatory markers and serum creatinine- Serum troponin T: 0.153 µg/L- Pro–B-type natriuretic protein: 654.5 pg/mL- Serial electrocardiograms: No ischemic ST changes- Bronchoalveolar lavage: 3 consecutive samples with increasing bloody return, total red blood cell count of 9000/µLImaging Studies:- Chest radiograph: Bilateral multiple nodular infiltrates  Image Title: Figure 1A - Chest radiograph on presentation  Description: Shows bilateral multiple nodular infiltrates- CT pulmonary angiogram: Negative for pulmonary embolism, showed bilateral patchy nodular opacitiesCardiac Studies:- Echocardiogram findings:  - Left ventricular ejection fraction: 15%  - Diffuse left ventricular hypokinesis  - Dilated LV cavity but preserved right ventricular function- Right heart catheterization: Low filling pressures and low cardiac index

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 59-year-old Japanese man presented with malaise and chills that began the day before his visit. Medical history included hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Four months prior, he was diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and had a history of perianal abscess during induction chemotherapy. The current admission was for maintenance chemotherapy with idarubicin and cytarabine. On day 10 of hospitalization, he experienced a 40.2°C fever, chills, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain when breathing deeply or coughing.

Vital signs:- Blood pressure: 122/74 mm Hg- Heart rate: 109 beats/min (consistently tachycardic)- Respiratory rate: 24 breaths/min- Oxygen saturation: 98% on room airPhysical findings:- Percussion tenderness in the right upper quadrant- Remainder of examination unremarkable

Laboratory Tests:- Blood count: Leukocyte count 0.1 × 10⁹/L (50% neutrophils), Thrombocytes 11.0 × 10⁹/L, Hemoglobin 8.0 g/L- Liver function: Total bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL, Aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L, Alkaline phosphatase 1065 U/L, γ-Glutamyl transpeptidase 168 U/LImaging Studies:- Image Title: Abdominal CT scan- Image Description: Multiple, small, circumscribed, hypoattenuating lesions in the liver and spleenMicrobiological Studies:- Blood cultures: Positive for yeast after 30 hours- Gram staining: Revealed arthroconidia and hyphal fungi- Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar: Dry cottony colonies with frosted glass appearance- Molecular identification: D1/D2 26S rDNA and internal transcribed spacer region of rRNA gene analysis performed- Drug susceptibility testing: MIC values - voriconazole 0.25 μg/mL, micafungin 4.0 μg/mL

A 51-year-old Hispanic man with a medical history of anxiety presented with 3 days of low back pain. Social history included active tobacco, alcohol, and marijuana use. Family history included prostate cancer (father), melanoma (brother), and colon cancer (niece).

Vital signs: blood pressure 160/80 mm Hg. Physical findings: right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and right paraspinal tenderness.

- Laboratory tests:     - Hyponatremia (129 mmol/L)    - Leukocytosis (13.0 × 10⁹/L)     - Urinalysis: 15 mg/dL ketones    - Total metanephrine: 246 pg/mL (high; normal ≤205)    - Normetanephrine: 246 pg/mL    - Estradiol: 246 pmol/L (high; normal <143)    - Normal levels: Morning cortisol, ACTH, aldosterone, renin, DHEA sulfate, testosterone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone    - Initial serum β-hCG: 691 IU/L (normal 0-5 IU/L), increased to 1860 IU/L on repeat    - AFP: undetectable- Imaging studies:    1. CT abdomen/pelvis:       Title: Initial abdominal CT       Description: Large 8.1 × 6.7 × 8.6 cm well-circumscribed right suprarenal retroperitoneal hemorrhagic mass-like density without active extravasation        2. MRI adrenal protocol:       Title: Adrenal MRI       Description: Right adrenal hemorrhagic mass measuring 9.9 × 9.0 × 6.8 cm with mass effect to the inferior vena cava and right kidney        3. Testicular ultrasound:       Description: No neoplasm identified        4. Chest CT:       Description: Numerous pulmonary nodules- Pathology:    - Poorly differentiated tumor composed of syncytial, intermediate in situ trophoblastic cells    - Immunostaining positive for AE1/AE3, CAM5.2, inhibin, β-hCG (strongly), Glypican-3 and PLAP (focally)    - Negative for CD30, CD117, AFP, OCT4, calretinin, synaptophysin, Melan-A, ERG, CAIX, PAX8, TTF-1, and S100    - Lymph nodes negative for malignancy

An 82-year-old man with a 60 pack-year history of tobacco use presented with progressive dysphagia, first to solids and then to liquids, over a three-month period. He experienced episodes of food getting stuck in his throat, weight loss of more than 100 lbs, night sweats, and hoarseness. A productive cough was noted, but there was no fever, chest pain, or hemoptysis.

Physical findings included:- Cachexia and exaggerated cervical lordosis- Normal lymph nodes- Tongue paralysis with atrophy on cranial nerve testing

1. Computed Tomography (CT) of neck:- Atrophy of the tongue- Large confluent anterior cervical osteophytes from C2–T1- Bilateral noncalcified pulmonary nodules at lung apices- Enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes2. CT of chest:- Diffuse innumerable pulmonary nodules predominantly in lung bases- Small mediastinal and hilar nodes3. Speech-Language Pathology Evaluation:- Modified barium swallow study showed:  * No epiglottic inversion  * Reduced laryngeal and hyoid excursion  * Reduced arytenoid movement  * Deep anterior wall aspiration  * Weak, delayed cough reflex4. Brain MRI:- Showed chronic ischemic changes, no acute abnormalities5. Cervical spine MRI:- Revealed multilevel bulky large anterior osteophytes6. Flexible laryngoscopy:- Large retropharyngeal mass partially obstructing airway- Mobile vocal cords bilaterally7. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD):- Extrinsic compression of upper esophagusImage Information:- Figure 1: CT scan showing large confluent anterior cervical osteophytes- Figure 2: MRI showing multilevel degenerative changes with bulky large anterior osteophytes- Figure 3: EGD showing bulging in upper esophagus with significant compression

strict_queue_context.vignette:
An 81-year-old man initially developed a cough, subjective fever, and shortness of breath. He was first treated with azithromycin for bronchitis, followed by levofloxacin after a right upper lobe infiltrate was found. His symptoms progressed despite antibiotics. Medical history includes coronary artery disease with coronary artery bypass (two years prior), atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c: 8.1%). He had spent time at a Northern Minnesota cabin but reported minimal outdoor exposure. Previous missionary work in Colombia ended two years before admission. Never smoked and rarely consumed alcohol.

Vital signs: Temperature 38.6°C, Pulse 130 beats/min, Blood Pressure 114/61 mm Hg, Respiratory Rate 22 breaths/min, Oxygen Saturation 82% (improved to >90% with 5 L/min oxygen). Lung sounds were diminished in the right upper lobe, with diffuse crackles in the right lung base. No clubbing or cyanosis. Cardiac examination showed tachycardic irregularly irregular rhythm, systolic ejection murmur, and mild pitting edema to the knee bilaterally. No cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Neurologic and skin examinations were normal. Later developed right-sided ptosis and anisocoria with an asymmetrically miotic right pupil (more evident in dark environment).

Laboratory Tests:
- Leukocytosis: 15,000/mm³
- Procalcitonin: 0.77 ng/mL
- Positive Blastomyces urine antigen
- Positive Histoplasmosis blood antigen
- Negative results for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
- Negative antigen tests for Cryptococcus, Legionella, and influenza
- Negative Paracoccidioides serum antibody

Imaging Studies:
1. Chest Radiograph
Title: Initial Chest Radiograph
Description: Dense consolidation of the right upper lobe, patchy nodular infiltrates of left upper lobe, 5-mm noncalcified rounded infiltrate in posterolateral left lower lobe

2. CT and MRI
Title: Emergency Head CT and Brain MRI
Description: Both showed no acute process

Other Tests:
Bronchoscopy findings: Moderate clear secretions with erythematous and edematous bronchial mucosa
Bronchoalveolar lavage: Spherical broadly based budding yeast on Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver stain

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 64-year-old woman with a 5-year history of diabetes mellitus, on maintenance dialysis for diabetic nephropathy for 2 years. Medical history included hypertension and breast cancer. One month prior to presentation, she experienced vomiting and diarrhea that resolved after approximately 1 week. Early in the presenting month, she slowly developed difficulty in moving extremities, low-volume voice, and slow speech. Symptoms progressed gradually, leading to difficulty in getting up or walking steadily.

Blood pressure: 163/76 mmHg. Neurological examination revealed:- No disturbance of consciousness- Mask-like face- Hypophonia- Bradykinesia- Rigidity of both upper limbs- Left terminal tremor- Weakness of proximal muscles in both lower limbs- Gait disturbance (short and shuffling steps, reduced arm swing)- Positive Babinski and Chaddock signs in left lower extremity

- Laboratory Tests:  * Blood tests showed no abnormalities  * Normal vitamin B1, thyroid function, and lactate levels  * Normal blood gas analysis without acidosis  * Normal spinal fluid test- Imaging Studies:  1. Brain MRI:     Title: T2-weighted brain MRI     Description: High-intensity areas in bilateral lenticular nucleus with lentiform fork sign    2. Diffusion-weighted imaging:     Description: Equal intensity    3. Dopamine transporter scan:     Description: No decreased accumulation, showed increased levels in the lesions    4. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS):     Description: Demonstrated a lactate peak    5. Arterial spin labeling (ASL):     Description: Showed hyperperfusion in the lesions

A 34-year-old woman with a history of severe obesity and unipolar major depression with psychotic features, on lurasidone (92.5mg/day) for four months. The evening prior to symptom onset, the patient completed a 5 km flat walk, which was unusual for her otherwise sedentary routine. Three days later, she presented to the emergency department with bilateral foot drop and painful swelling of the legs.

Patient presented with:- Bilateral peroneal nerve paralysis- Hardened painful forelegs- Visibly swollen and reddish colored legs- Temperature: 37.9°C

Laboratory Tests:- CRP: 280mg/dL- WBC: 25,000/μL- Neutrophils: 20,000/μL- CPK: 15,000U/L- GOT: 409U/L- GPT: 152U/L- LDH: 1322U/LImaging Studies:1. Emergency Echographic Assessment:- Showed indirect signs of myositis and panniculitis- Main arteries and veins of both lower limbs were patent2. Electroneurography (ENG):- Showed bilateral motor nerve block below the fibular head3. Electromyography (EMG):- No signs of spontaneous nor voluntary activity in peroneal innervated muscles4. MRI Findings:Image Title: Magnetic resonance imaging of leg musclesImage Description: - Rounded morphology of both peroneal muscle compartments- Outward convex bulging of the overlying crural fascia- Muscle edema- Area of necrosis in both tibialis anterior muscles

A 30-year-old male presented with a 6-year history of recurrent respiratory symptoms and acute exacerbation with dyspnea for 1 day. Past medical history included hospitalization in intensive care unit one year ago requiring mechanical ventilation for over 10 days. Prior pulmonary function tests showed severe mixed ventilation dysfunction with FEV1 PreD of 26% and FEV1/FVC percent of 56%. Patient had previously scored 9 on the Asthma Control Test and 6 on the Asthma Control Questionnaire.

Vital signs on admission:- Temperature: 35.5°C- Pulse: 121 beats/min- Respiratory rate: 32 times/min- Blood pressure: 169/100 mmHg- SpO2: 83% (without oxygen)Physical findings:- Orthopnea- Cyanosis of the lips- Profuse sweating- Three-concave sign- Hyperresonance in percussion of both lungs- Accelerated respiration- Loud and diffuse wheezing rales in both lungs

Laboratory Tests:- Blood gas analysis: pH 7.137, PCO2 74.7 mmHg, PO2 95.0 mmHg, SO2 94.0%, FiO2 41.0%, oxygenation index 232 mmHg- Complete blood count: WBC 15.51 × 109/L, neutrophil percentage 74.2%, eosinophil percentage 7.2%- Other biochemical and coagulation parameters were normalImaging Studies:- Chest CT  Title: Chest CT examination  Description: No major abnormalities observed in both lungs and heartPulmonary Function Tests:- Bronchodilator test: increase in absolute FEV1 of 250 mL, improvement rate of 24%- Follow-up tests showed FEV1: 2.2L, FVC: 3.77L, FEV1%pred: 56.9%, FEV1/FVC%: 69.8%, PEF: 5.88L/s

strict_queue_context.vignette:
An 80-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to the emergency department with progressive shortness of breath for one day duration, accompanied by chest tightness and non-radiating retrosternal chest pain. The patient denied previous episodes of chest pain, and no other relevant associated symptoms were previously noticed.

Initial vital signs showed blood pressure of 191/99 mmHg, heart rate of 114 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 68% under ambient air. The patient was slightly drowsy but conversant and oriented. Breathing sounds were bilaterally coarse upon auscultation. Normal heart sounds without obvious murmurs or pericardial rubs were recorded. The remainder of the systemic physical examination results were unremarkable.

- Laboratory Tests: Serial Troponin-T measurements showed progressive elevation, reaching 1101 ng/L on day 4.- Imaging Studies:  1. Chest Radiography     Title: Initial chest X-ray     Description: Bilateral fine reticular opacities, widened mediastinum, cardiomegaly, and bilateral blunted costophrenic angles    2. Electrocardiogram (EKG)     Description: Sinus tachycardia with mildly elevated ST-segments at the inferior leads    3. Echocardiography     Description: Normal left atrial and ventricular sizes, good left ventricular contractility, no pericardial effusion or regional wall motion abnormalities    4. CT Angiography     Description: Right anterior mediastinal mass, well demarcated with minimal contact with surrounding great vessels and no adjoining abnormal lymph nodes    5. Coronary Angiography     Description: Diffusely slow coronary flow with patency in all three coronary arteries    6. Biopsy Results     Description: Epithelial malignancy of thymic origin, showing ovoid-to spindle neoplastic cells with nuclear atypia and mitosis

Abnormal perfusion of liver parenchyma around lesion in arterial phase. Honeycomb enhancement in delayed phase.2. Abdominal MRI:- Title: Abdominal MRI of liver lesion- Description: Mass shadow with mixed signal in SIV segment of liver, measuring 55mm × 42mm × 64mm. Honeycomb-like enhancement with narrow-band edema signals.Genetic Testing:- Heterozygous mutation in exon 3 of the ELANE genePathology:- Liver tissue showed scattered hepatic structures with focal abscess changes- Culture from liver lesion: Positive for Staphylococcus aureus

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 4-year-old female was initially referred to the Genetics department at 20 days of age. At 21 months, she experienced weekly recurrent episodes of fixed gaze, absence-like loss of contact, and myoclonic-like movements of upper and lower arms lasting from a few seconds to 15 minutes, with frequent falls. Development history showed gross motor development was adequate, but fine motor, language, and sociability skills were at the level of 16 months. Family history includes mother with moderate intellectual disability and childhood-onset epilepsy, maternal grandmother with late-onset epilepsy, and maternal aunt with mild intellectual impairment.

Physical examination revealed normal tonus and reflexes, mild psychomotor delay, and broad-based gait. Notable features included: hypotonic face, high frontal hairline, thin long eyebrows with lateral extension and medial flare, marked epicanthus inversus, upslanting palpebral fissures, round nostrils, full cheeks, protruding lower lip, apparently low-set and posteriorly rotated ears with up-lifted ear lobes, simple descending helix, protruding descending anthelix, increased intermamillary distance, mild pectus excavatum, atypical hemangiomas over the chest left and on the inside of left upper arm, 5th-finger clinodactyly, and a broad 1st toe. Growth parameters: weight 12,600g (80th centile), length 89cm (90th centile), and OFC 46.6cm (25th centile, relative microcephaly).

- Laboratory Tests: All routine hematological, biochemical, and thyroid tests were normal.
- Imaging Studies:
  * Brain MRI showed mild frontal colpocephaly
- Other Tests:
  * Sleep-deprived electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal
  * Ophthalmological examination revealed mild hyperopia, intermittent strabismus and nystagmus of congenital origin
  * Otolaryngological and cardiological tests were normal
- Genetic Tests:
  * Cytogenetic analysis revealed 46,XX,inv(16)(q22.3q24.1)mat
  * Microarray analysis showed no cryptic microdeletions or microduplications
  * Clinical Exome Sequencing detected a pathogenic nonsense variant in the CHD2 gene [NM_001271.4:c.5035C>T p.(Arg1679Ter)]

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 13-year-old boy presented with a five-day history of left scrotal soreness and oedema. The patient had no lower urinary tract symptoms and no major relevant medical or surgical history. Based on penile characteristics, the patient was diagnosed with occult penis. Other congenital anomalies of the genitourinary tract were excluded based on imaging findings.

Scrotal investigation revealed an enlarged testis, epididymis, and infected appendages. No torsion was evident in the sperm vessels; however, purulent foci were visible on the surface of the vessels, and their texture was tough and inseparable. The patient was at Tanner stage G4P4.

- Laboratory tests: Blood workup showed mild leukocytosis (18.5 × 109/L). Urine analysis was negative. Pus culture isolated P. aeruginosa, susceptible to ceftazidime and ofloxacin.- Imaging studies:  1. Doppler ultrasonography: Revealed an enlarged left testis with heterogeneous echo pattern, enhanced vascularity, and retained testicular blood flow.  2. Follow-up sonography: Showed heterogeneous echotexture in the left testis and epididymis, with a mild whirlpool sign and hyperechogenicity in the inguinal area.  3. MRI Image (at 60 days):     Title: MR imaging of testes     Description: Left testis showed no enhancement in T2, indicating disappearance of the left testis.- Pathological examination: Showed hemorrhagic infarction of the left testicular appendage and fibrocystic-like tissue with inflammatory cell infiltration.

A 42-year-old Caucasian man with a 12-year history of well-controlled HIV (undetectable viral load, CD4+ count 1184 × 10^6 cell/liter). Past medical history includes treatment for early latent syphilis six years prior. The patient presented with low-grade fever (37.5°) and sudden appearance of skin lesions at the base of his penis. He reported recent sexual activity with multiple male partners. Two days after the initial skin manifestations, he developed fever up to 39°C, chest pain without irradiation, and shortness of breath.

Initial examination revealed vesicular and umbilicated lesions on genitals and small lymphadenomegaly in the groin area. No oropharyngeal lesions were detected. Upon admission for chest symptoms, the patient was hemodynamically stable with continuous anterior chest pain exacerbated by deep breathing.

- Laboratory Tests:    * High-sensitivity cardiac troponin: 128.00 pg/ml initially, peaked at 142.00 pg/ml (reference value < 14 pg/ml)    * Multiple viral serologies including CMV, EBV, Coxsackievirus, Echovirus, Parvovirus B19, and Herpes virus 1/2 were negative (except for past CMV and EBV exposure)    - Imaging Studies:    * ECG: Showed sinus tachycardia with elevated PR segment in aVR lead and depressed in peripheral and thoracic leads    * Echocardiography: Left ventricle diastolic diameter of 59 mm, hypokinetic left ventricle with EF 50%    * Chest CT angiography: Normal, no pulmonary embolism or pneumonia    * Cardiac MRI: Showed slightly increased global T1 and T2 mapping values, minimal hyperintensity of pericardium without effusion, normal biventricular function (EF 57%)    * Coronary CT angiography: Normal    - Continuous Monitoring:    * ECG monitoring showed persistent episodes of sinus pauses (longest 10.1 seconds)    * Episodes of advanced AV block grade 2 Mobitz type 1 and 2    * Sinus bradycardia (heart rate 40-45, nadir 32 pulses/minute while sleeping)

A patient in their 80s presented with dyspnea and syncope during exercise. Medical history included essential hypertension and Parkinson disease. The patient reported experiencing dyspnea on exertion and exercise intolerance for the past year, with difficulty walking more than 100m. They also experienced syncope during a bicycle ride with loss of consciousness for a few minutes, followed by complete recovery.

Vital signs were normal except for elevated blood pressure of 150/78 mm Hg. Chest auscultation revealed normal breath and heart sounds without any murmurs.

- Laboratory tests: Hemogram, serum electrolytes, and thyroid function test were within normal limits.- Echocardiogram findings:  - Normal left ventricular ejection fraction (74%)  - Normal wall motion  - Left atrial enlargement (volume index, 34.89 mL/m2)  - Uncertain diastolic function  - No significant valvular abnormality  - Pulmonary hypertension (mean pulmonary arterial pressure 32 mm Hg)- ECG findings:  Image Title: Initial ECG  Image Description: Shows sinus rhythm with first-degree atrioventricular block (PR interval 360 ms), right bundle-branch block (RBBB) and left anterior fascicular block (LAFB). Wide QRS complex (120 ms), rSR in lead V1, and RS in lead V6 (deep and wide S waves ≥40 ms). Left axis deviation and qR in leads I and aVL, and rS in leads II, III, and aVF.- 24-hour ECG monitoring:  Image Title: Continuous ambulatory ECG monitoring  Image Description: Shows sinus rhythm (average 60 beats/min), PR prolongation (360 ms) and third-degree AV block with minimum heart rate of 36 beats/min. Mobitz type I second-degree AV block with pause and junctional escape beat observed. No atrial/ventricular arrhythmia found.

strict_queue_context.reference_diagnosis: Linear or annular lupus erythematosus panniculitis of the scalp (LALPS)
strict_queue_context.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.

Examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow. The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Dermoscopic examination of the alopecic area revealed several short vellus hairs, yellow dots, and honeycomb hyperpigmentation; however, broken hairs were not seen. The result of a hair pull test was negative.

- Histopathologic examination:    Image A: Clinical image of annular arc from a longitudinally furrowed skin lesion on the left eyebrow and forehead to an alopecic lesion    Image B: Clinical image of the bandlike grooved alopecic lesion on the left side of the frontal scalp and vertex    Image C: Scanning view shows predominant lymphocytic infiltrates in perifollicular and periappendageal regions of the dermis and lobular panniculitis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)    Image D: High-power view shows inflammatory infiltrates between adipocytes with hyaline fat necrosis in the subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)  - Laboratory findings:    - Direct immunofluorescence: Positive with granular deposition of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and fibrinogen in the dermal blood vessels    - Antinuclear antibody: Negative    - Antidouble-stranded DNA antibody: Negative    - All other laboratory test findings were normal

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A male patient in his 20s presented with a 12-month history of asymptomatic red to brown macules and papules that initially appeared on his trunk and subsequently spread to the upper and proximal lower extremities. The lesions were symmetrically distributed and did not coalesce. His face, distal extremities, and mucous membranes were unaffected. The patient reported that some lesions had resolved spontaneously with residual hyperpigmentation. His medical history was unremarkable, and he did not take any medication on a regular basis.

- Multiple red to brown macules and papules on trunk and extremities- Symmetrically distributed lesions that did not coalesce- Face, distal extremities, and mucous membranes unaffected- No lymphadenopathy- Other systems review unremarkable

Laboratory Tests:- Blood cell count showed hypereosinophilia (4220/μL; reference range 50-250/μL)- Elevated tryptase (33.7 ng/mL; reference range <11.5 ng/mL)- Elevated vitamin B12 (>6000 pg/mL; reference range 211-911 pg/mL)- Negative serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis A, B, and C- Negative tests for parasitic infectionsImaging Studies:- CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis: no pathologic findings- Cranial MRI: no pathologic findingsPathological Findings:- Skin biopsy (chest and upper extremity):  - Nodular infiltration of histiocytes with lymphocytes and eosinophils in upper dermis  - No lipid-laden foam cells or multinucleated giant cells  - Immunohistochemistry: CD68 positive, stabilin 1 positive, S-100 protein weakly positive, CD1a negativeBone Marrow Analysis:- Hypercellularity with myeloid hyperplasia- Increased eosinophils (20%, reference range <5%)- FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene positive on RT-PCR

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A woman in her 40s presented with blurred vision in the right eye. She was undergoing treatment with systemic steroids, durvalumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor), and bevacizumab. Ten days after initial presentation, the patient developed sudden vision loss in the right eye.

Initial examination: Visual acuity of 20/25 OU. Right eye showed full visual field, right-sided relative afferent pupillary defect, unremarkable anterior segment, and mild swelling of the optic disc. Left eye had normal fundus and visual function. Follow-up examination (after vision loss): Right eye showed no light perception vision, marked swelling of the optic disc, peripapillary retinal hemorrhages, and occlusion of the superior branch artery. Two days later: Combined occlusion of the central retinal artery and vein, and a new collection of whitish material suspended anterior to the optic disc, forming a pocket in the posterior vitreous.

- Imaging Studies:    Image Title: MRI at Onset of Vision Loss    Image Description:     - Coronal T1-weighted contrast-enhanced image: Focal enhancement along enlarged right optic nerve    - Axial T1-weighted contrast-enhanced image: Diffuse enlargement of orbital portion of right optic nerve, enhancement of nerve sheath, slight flattening of posterior globe    - Coronal T2-weighted (FLAIR) image: Hyperintensity of right optic nerve  - Laboratory Tests:    - Lumbar puncture showed no abnormalities      - Other Tests:    - Wide-field fluorescein angiography: Showed choroidal flush but complete lack of perfusion of retinal vasculature      - Pathological Examination:    - Vitreous biopsy: Hypercellular sample with astrocytic neoplasm, small to medium-sized cells with scant cytoplasm and oval, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei    - Immunohistochemistry: Positive for glial fibrillary acid protein, oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2, mutant IDH-1 protein, p53; Loss of ATRX protein; Ki-67 proliferation index ~10%

A 50-year-old male patient was brought to the emergency department due to syncope 30 minutes before admission. The patient reported experiencing palpitation and amaurosis, followed by loss of consciousness that lasted for several minutes, without any preceding body position change, cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath. The patient experienced a previous episode of syncope 1 month prior. Medical history indicated only diabetes, which was well controlled with medication.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
An obese man in his mid-30s with no prior systemic or ocular disorders presented to a local emergency department after waking with vision loss in his right eye. The night prior, he had been drinking alcohol heavily and took 2 buprenorphine hydrochloride/naloxone hydrochloride pills. He denied any trauma. He also experienced pain, numbness, and erythematous induration of his right eyelids and forearm that increased throughout the day.

Visual acuity: No light perception in right eye (OD) and 20/20 in left eye (OS). Right eye showed tense eyelid edema, chemosis, corneal haze, and restricted motility in all fields of gaze. Right pupil was mid-dilated with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure was 37 mm Hg OD and 21 mm Hg OS. Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed tortuous vessels, serous retinal detachment sparing the inferior periphery, and macular whitening. Left eye examination was normal.

- Laboratory Tests:
Creatinine level: 2.2 mg/dL
Creatine kinase level: 29,320 U/L

- Imaging Studies:
1. Noncontrast computed tomography of head and orbits: Showed periorbital soft-tissue swelling

2. Optical Coherence Tomography:
Image Title: OCT of the Right Eye
Image Description: Demonstrates severe disorganization of the retinal architecture, subretinal fluid, and sub-retinal pigment epithelial fluid

3. Fluorescein Angiography:
Image Title: Fluorescein Angiography of the Right Eye
Image Description: Shows delayed choroidal filling, delayed retinal arterial filling, patchy temporal hyperfluorescence, diffuse leakage and poor vascular perfusion in various phases

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 78-year-old man presented with painful swelling and ulceration of the glans penis of 1 month's duration. His medical history included an elevated white blood cell count and inguinal lymphadenopathy discovered 9 years prior. Four years after initial presentation, he experienced fatigue, weight loss, and loss of appetite. The current illness began 1 month prior to admission when he noticed asymptomatic 'green-yellow welts' and swelling of the glans penis. The swelling became progressively painful and evolved to the size of an 'orange' over 4 days. Previous treatments with topical antibiotics, antifungal agents, hydrogen peroxide soaks, warm compresses, and cephalexin showed no improvement.

Patient appeared healthy. The glans penis and corona were grossly edematous, with a 3.7 × 3.3-cm tender, firm ulcer on the ventral surface of the penis with overlying black eschar, adherent yellow crust, and granulation tissue. No urethral discharge was present.

- Laboratory Tests: Routine blood test results were within normal limits. Cultures, assays, and blood tests evaluating for viral, bacterial, or fungal etiology were negative.

- Pathology Studies: Biopsy of the glans penis ulcer showed dermal infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes, which were CD20+, CD79a+, and CD5+, within the background of a reactive T-cell infiltrate. PCR analysis revealed a clonal IgH gene rearrangement.

- Imaging Studies: PET-CT scan demonstrated FDG-avid abdominal and peripancreatic lymph nodes.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A woman in her 50s presented with 4 days of blurry vision and pain in her left eye after undergoing a routine dental cleaning 1 week prior. She had no history of gingival disease or cavities. Her medical and ocular histories were unremarkable.

Visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/50 OS. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Left eye examination showed conjunctival hyperemia, faint keratic precipitates, 3+ cells with fibrin in the anterior chamber, mild nuclear sclerosis, and a whitish focal granuloma at the 4-o'clock position at the pupillary margin. The posterior segment was unremarkable, with no evidence of vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis. The right eye was unremarkable. At 1-day follow-up, visual acuity declined to 20/100 OS, with development of hypopyon and increased fibrinous material emanating from the iris lesion. No posterior segment involvement was noted.

- Microscopy: Gram stain revealed gram-positive cocci in chains and gram-positive rods in a branching pattern.  Image Title: Gram Stain of Iris Abscess  Image Description: Mixed flora of gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains and gram-positive bacilli (original magnification ×400)- Cultures: Aerobic culture revealed Streptococcus intermedius. The gram-positive bacilli could not be identified more specifically.- Additional Tests: Blood and urine cultures, electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were unremarkable.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 13-year-old boy presented with an intensely pruritic skin eruption that appeared approximately 24 hours after intensive sun exposure in spring. The patient was otherwise healthy but reported an episode of malaise and headache 2 weeks before first presentation. He had no history of photosensitivity, and denied the use of any topical or systemic photosensitizers.

Erythema and helical thickening as well as numerous small blisters, 2 to 3 mm in diameter, were present on both ears. Similar vesicles were observed at the upper and lower vermillion border. Several erythematous papules and crusts were located on the cheeks, neck, and lower arms.

- Laboratory tests: Differential blood count, routine chemical analysis, and serum porphyrins were unremarkable. Serum parvovirus B19 (PVB19) IgM and IgG antibodies were detectable. Bacterial cultures from blister fluid were unremarkable.- Virologic analyses: Negative results for herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, hepatitis B and C viruses, 8 human polyomaviruses, and enteroviruses. PVB19 DNA was found (viral load of 0.2 PVB19 DNA copies/β-globin gene copy, or 33,438 copies/μg of isolated DNA) in lesional skin biopsy specimen, but not in the serum.- Other tests: Standard phototesting with UV-A and UV-B was unremarkable.- Images:  Image 1 Title: The Patient's Clinical Findings on the Ears at First Presentation  Image 1 Description: Helical thickening, erythema, and numerous small vesicles are present on both ears  Image 2 Title: The Patient's Facial Lesions  Image 2 Description: Crusted papules and small erosions are located on the cheeks. Several blisters are located at the upper and lower vermillion border

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A man in his 70s presented to the emergency department with progressive dyspnea on exertion. His medical history includes multiple prior cardiac events and lung cancer with metastatic disease to the brain and myocardium. Ten months prior, he had received 2 drug-eluting stents to the right coronary artery. At presentation, the patient denied chest pain.

No detailed physical examination findings were provided in the case report.

- Laboratory tests: High-sensitivity cardiac troponin-T (hs-cTnT) level was 40 ng/L (reference range, 0-14 ng/L), unchanged from baseline value obtained 1 month prior.- ECG findings:   - Normal sinus rhythm at 90 beats per minute  - 1.0-mm ST elevation in lead V1  - 4.0-mm ST elevation in leads V2 and V3   - T-wave inversions in leads I, aVL, V4, V5, and V6  - Diffusely low voltages in both limb leads and precordial leads  - Imaging studies:  1. Transthoracic echocardiogram:     Image Title: Apical 4-chamber view     Image Description: Well-circumscribed 2.8 × 2.6-cm mass located in the left ventricular mid-apical anteroseptum     Additional findings:      - Preserved left ventricular systolic function     - No regional wall motion abnormalities     - Large pericardial effusion with signs of impending cardiac tamponade  2. Coronary angiography:     Findings: Nonobstructive epicardial coronary artery disease without evidence of acute thrombotic or embolic occlusion

strict_queue_context.reference_diagnosis: Drug-induced dermatomyositis secondary to ipilimumab therapy
strict_queue_context.vignette:
A woman in her 50s with stage IV B-RAF V600E mutant malignant melanoma with metastases of the liver, lungs, and peritoneum (primary site unknown). Within 2 weeks of starting ipilimumab treatment, she developed skin symptoms. After initial improvement and later disease recurrence, she received a second course of ipilimumab 14 months later, which led to recurrence and worsening of symptoms.

Physical findings included:- Photodistributed erythematous to violaceous eruption- Diffuse erythema of forehead and midface, involving nasolabial folds- Erythema and edema of upper eyelids- Diffuse erythema of upper chest and upper back- Flagellate erythema on posterior neck- Flat-topped pink to erythematous papules over knuckles- Prominent erythema at nailfolds with dilated capillary loops, capillary dropout, and ragged cuticles- Grade 4/5 strength on resisted abduction of shoulders bilaterally- Limited flexion of both hips- Reduced activity level due to weakness and early fatigue

Laboratory Tests:- Creatine kinase: 1088 U/L (increased to 1854 U/L)- Aldolase: 23.0 U/L- C-reactive protein: 28.6 mg/L- Antinuclear antibody titer: 1:640 with speckled pattern- Jo-1 antibody: negativeImaging Studies:- MRI showed mild short TI inversion recovery hyperintensity of bilateral vastus lateralis and rectus femoris musclesBiopsy Results:- Vastus lateralis muscle biopsy showed atrophy of type II muscle fibers without evidence of inflammatory myositis (note: performed after corticosteroid treatment)

strict_queue_context.reference_diagnosis: Anastrozole-associated uveitis with cystoid macular edema
strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 65-year-old woman presented with blurry vision in her right eye for several months. Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. Patient had undergone left-sided mastectomy 2.5 years prior and had been on anastrozole therapy for more than 2 years. Medical history and past medication use were otherwise unremarkable.

Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/150 OS without improvement on pinhole testing. Intraocular pressures were normal. Right eye showed trace conjunctival injection without definite ciliary flush, 2+ fine keratic precipitates, and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Left eye had a few keratic precipitates. Dilated fundus examination revealed cystoid macular edema with a yellow spot in the fovea in the right eye and an epiretinal membrane in the left eye. No inflammation in the periphery was noted in either eye.

- Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):  Image Title: OCT Scans  Image Description: Right eye showed significant cystoid macular edema and subfoveal fluid. Left eye had a mild epiretinal membrane.- Fluorescein Angiography:  Image Title: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography  Image Description: Revealed cystoid macular edema with leakage in both right and left eyes.- Blood Tests: Tests for vasculitis and rheumatologic disorders were within reference limits. Normal findings for tick-borne and bacterial diseases.- Imaging:  Computed tomography of the chest was unremarkable.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 9-year-old girl with a small muscular ventricular septal defect presented with chest pain and dyspnea one week after recovering from an upper respiratory infection and after minor anterior chest trauma in a fall. She was afebrile. Heart rate was 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, blood pressure 113/66 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation normal. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness over the sternum and normal cardiac auscultation. 

Chest radiography showed mild cardiomediastinal silhouette enlargement and a focal opacity in the right middle lung. ECG was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse, normal biventricular systolic function, and no ventricular septal defect. 

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 1,570 cells/µL (normal 40–190), C-reactive protein 1.94 mg/dL (normal <0.5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/hr (normal 0–30), and troponin T 0.25 ng/mL (normal <0.1). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed elevated global myocardial T2 (70 ms) and T1 (1150 ms) values, increased left ventricular wall thickness, a moderate pericardial effusion, and no late gadolinium enhancement.

She was admitted with a working diagnosis of viral myopericarditis. Treatment with oral ibuprofen and colchicine resulted in resolution of chest pain, normalization of troponin and inflammatory markers, and reduction of the pericardial effusion over three days. However, the absolute eosinophil count rose further. Consultations with infectious diseases, allergy/immunology, and rheumatology were obtained. Further history elicited pica and exposure to two dogs and a cat. 

Chest computed tomography revealed multiple pulmonary nodules with adjacent ground-glass opacities. An infectious workup showed negative PCR tests for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, rhinovirus, and adenovirus; negative Bartonella henselae titers; and a negative T-SPOT tuberculosis test. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and IgG were elevated, but nasopharyngeal Mycoplasma PCR was negative. Toxocara serology was sent and was pending at discharge.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 53-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and bipolar disorder was admitted for a 4-week history of progressive asthenia, anorexia, and a 7-kg weight loss, with vomiting during the last 2 days. On examination, her BMI was 18.2 kg/m2 and she was obnubilated; the ECG was normal. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum calcium 3.8 mmol/L (normal phosphorus), nonregenerative normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), and acute functional renal failure (creatinine clearance 30 mL/min).  
• PTH 9 ng/L.  
• Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; negative 24-hour proteinuria; no monoclonal peak on serum or urine immunoelectrophoresis; normal serum free light-chain ratio.  

She received IV saline and one dose of zoledronate, with normalization of calcium and renal function by day 3. A CT scan of the body showed two osteolytic lesions of the left frontal and temporal skull bones, multiple hypodense micronodules in all hepatic segments, and multiple splenic nodules. Brain MRI demonstrated T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, gadolinium-enhancing lesions in the same skull regions. A DEXA scan revealed osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score –2.4). Mammography, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal. Bone marrow biopsy and labial salivary gland histology were unremarkable. A percutaneous fine-needle aspiration of the liver showed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis without malignancy. The intradermal tuberculin test was negative. During this period, hypercalcemia recurred, and two additional doses of zoledronate were administered 15 days apart despite initial correction.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 34-year-old man with hypertension on dual antihypertensive therapy, well followed by nephrology, presented to the emergency department with acute onset epigastric pain. He described the pain as continuous, burning, non-radiating, and of moderate intensity. His blood pressure was 200/84 mm Hg; all other vital signs were normal. On examination, he had epigastric tenderness without other abnormalities. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with signs of left ventricular hypertrophy. Routine blood tests, including troponin, were normal. While awaiting laboratory results, a point-of-care ultrasound was performed to evaluate the gallbladder; it showed a normal gallbladder without gallstones, no wall thickening, and no pericholecystic fluid. Subsequent cardiac windows revealed a small pericardial effusion.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 5‐year‐9‐month‐old, 170‐kg domestic llama mare was referred for a 1‐week history of dyspnea and inspiratory noise. The owner reported that an esophageal obstruction had been suspected by the referring veterinarian, but spasmolytics and passage of a gastric tube did not improve the signs. On presentation, the llama was bright, alert, in good condition (body‐condition score 3.5/5) with normal vital signs. In the middle third of the ventral cervical region, there was a 10 × 8 × 3‐cm subcutaneous mass that was partially firm and fluctuant, slightly painful, and mildly warm; the overlying skin appeared normal. No dysphagia, other masses, or lymphadenopathy were detected. A CBC showed mild leukocytosis (23,690/µL; reference 8,700–17,500/µL) with neutrophilia (92.4%; reference 42.4–76.4%) and lymphopenia (3.0%; reference 7.0–32.5%); eosinophils were decreased; hematocrit was 39.8% (reference 27.0–39.0%), MCV was mildly increased, and MCHC was mildly decreased. Flexible endoscopy of the esophagus and trachea under sedation revealed no abnormalities. Cervical ultrasonography showed a well‐demarcated, heterogeneously echogenic, encapsulated mass with no communication with the trachea or esophagus and no intrinsic vascular flow. Thoracic and cervical radiographs demonstrated a ventral soft‐tissue‐density mass in the mid‐to‐caudal cervical region causing a mild mass effect on the trachea; no pulmonary lesions or further abnormalities were noted.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 70‐year‐old woman with an undifferentiated connective tissue disorder and rheumatoid arthritis was treated with hydroxychloroquine in 2010, after which she developed a severe generalized bullous and pustular rash that resolved over three months following drug discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy. In 2022, hydroxychloroquine was restarted for her rheumatoid arthritis. Three days after restarting the drug, she was admitted with widespread erythema, desquamation, and pustulation. She denied any history of psoriasis. Laboratory studies revealed marked leukocytosis, hyperglycemia, hypoproteinemia, transaminitis, and an elevated C‐reactive protein level. Skin biopsies from the back demonstrated separation of the stratum corneum with multifocal subcorneal collections of neutrophils, underlying spongiotic epidermis with neutrophilic exocytosis, papillary dermal edema, and a superficial perivascular and interstitial infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and rare eosinophils.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 24-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive left hip pain radiating to the anterior thigh. The pain began as a dull aching groin discomfort, worsened over weeks, was severe at night, and was associated with weight loss and anorexia. There was no history of trauma. 

On examination, he had an antalgic gait, reduced range of motion of the left hip in all planes with spasms, and tenderness deep in the left groin. Straight-leg raising was negative, and neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. A pelvic radiograph was unremarkable. Initial MRI of the left hip showed synovitis and marrow edema without fracture. He received 6 months of empirical anti-tubercular therapy without clinical improvement.

An open synovial biopsy was performed; all cultures were negative, and histology showed mild to moderate chronic synovitis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates. Rheumatologic evaluation, including serologic studies, was unremarkable. A repeat MRI of the hips demonstrated a well-defined T1-hypointense, STIR-hyperintense lesion with a thick sclerotic rim in the anterolateral cortex of the left femoral head, associated marrow edema, moderate joint effusion, and synovitis.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 21-year-old man with no past medical or surgical history presented with a tender, palpable mass in his left buttock that he had noticed for several years but which had rapidly enlarged over the previous six months. He also reported recent onset of constipation and numbness of the left lower extremity, worsened by sitting. He denied any drainage, redness, fever, or systemic symptoms. He took no medications and had no family history of cancer.

On examination, a 4 × 4 cm tender mass was palpated in the left perineum without overlying skin changes. Neurologic examination showed hypoesthesia in the L5–S4 distribution on the left with intact motor function; the right lower extremity was normal. Abdominal and digital rectal examinations were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed a well-defined, nonenhancing, unilocular hypodense cystic lesion anterior to the rectum measuring 7.0 × 9.0 cm, as well as a separate 4.4 × 4.7 cm cyst in the left perineum. On contrast-enhanced MRI, both lesions appeared homogeneous, T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, and showed no wall enhancement. The cysts were distinct from the bladder, urethra, prostate, and rectum, and were suggested to have a narrow neck traversing the pelvic floor near the pudendal canal.
