strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 4-year-old girl of Turkish ancestry was brought to the emergency department for progressive unsteadiness and recurrent falls over the preceding 5 days. Five days earlier she had first noted staggering and grabbing for support to avoid falls; during her initial fall she sustained a nasal bridge laceration that required suturing. There was no prior medical history. On examination she was alert (GCS 15), afebrile, and appeared well; the nasal bridge wound was clean. Both external ear canals were obstructed by effusion and cerumen; the remainder of the neurologic and physical examination, including cranial-nerve testing, was age-appropriate. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
 Three-month history of “ear problems” was elicited: initial diagnosis of otitis media with effusion and tympanic perforation treated with antibiotics led to partial resolution. On current otoscopic examination, the left tympanic membrane was intact without effusion; the right external canal was occluded by polypoid tissue and purulent secretion. A Frenzel’s examination showed no nystagmus.  
 Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and temporal bones revealed bilateral osteolysis of the mastoids, superior and lateral semicircular canals, and the right external auditory canal, plus a separate osteolytic lesion in the dorsal left parietal bone. There was also adenoid hypertrophy and mild sinus mucosal thickening.  
 Brainstem evoked response audiometry demonstrated a threshold of 40 dB with normal wave latencies on the left and an 80 dB threshold with prolonged wave I latency on the right, indicating profound right-sided hearing loss.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
An 86-year-old woman with a history of dementia, living in a non–air-conditioned room during a heat wave, was found unconscious and brought to the emergency department. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 6 (E1V1M4), body temperature 42.4 °C, blood pressure 88/40 mm Hg, and pulse rate 120 beats/min. Laboratory studies revealed hepatic dysfunction, renal dysfunction, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Head MRI and MRA showed no abnormality. She was diagnosed with severe heat stroke (APACHE II score 42, SOFA score 15), intubated, and treated with extracorporeal cooling, fluid resuscitation, and DIC therapy; fursultiamine and levothyroxine were also given. Despite treatment, she remained unconscious. On day 6, brain MRI showed bilateral cerebellar hemisphere high-signal intensity on diffusion-weighted and FLAIR images with corresponding low ADC signals. On day 9, SPECT with 123I-IMP demonstrated decreased perfusion in the right cerebellar hemisphere. By day 13, MRI abnormalities had begun to improve, and her level of consciousness improved to E4VTM6.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use was transferred for evaluation of altered mental status. He was found minimally responsive and arrived febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10), requiring intubation for airway protection. On examination, he had left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5) without meningeal signs. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL). Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates. 

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema, scattered small foci of restricted diffusion, and subtle punctate blooming on susceptibility-weighted images; there was no enhancement after gadolinium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³ (57% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 81 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (serum 121 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative. Initial CSF studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli, herpes simplex virus PCR, and fungi. Empirical IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were begun; his leukocytosis improved but fever persisted. 

On hospital day 5 he became more obtunded. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 123 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 105 mg/dL), and no red cells. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement. 

Because the etiology remained unclear and the patient was deteriorating, a brain biopsy was planned.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. He reported ingestion and insufflation of “bath salts,” a history later confirmed by his family. He denied other medications or supplements and had no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 107°F, blood pressure 91/52 mm Hg, and pulse 93/min. He was confused and intermittently agitated, with pupils 3 mm and equal. Cardiovascular exam showed weak peripheral pulses without jugular venous distention or murmurs; lungs were clear; abdomen was soft; no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Urine toxicology detected only lorazepam and cotinine but was negative for over 80 other substances, including cannabinoids, cocaine, ecstasy, ephedrine, lysergide, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, oxycodone, and phencyclidine.

Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. Urine output was 4200 mL over the first 24 hours, then declined to 825 mL and 150 mL over subsequent 24-hour periods. He was started on daily hemodialysis for volume control and solute clearance.

Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin were started for presumed community-acquired pneumonia. On hospital day 2, a punch biopsy of a skin lesion revealed superficial and deep dermal thrombotic paucicellular vasculopathy involving skin appendages without significant neutrophils or leukocytoclasia. Tests for cryoglobulin, protein C, protein S, rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, complement levels, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies were negative. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:160; lupus anticoagulant was prolonged at 82 seconds (reference range, 27–41); anticardiolipin IgM was 64 (reference range, 0–12); and anti–phosphatidylserine IgM was >100 (reference range, <10). Nasopharyngeal testing for influenza antigen, streptococcal antigen, and Legionella antigen was negative. A FilmArray respiratory panel was positive for respiratory syncytial virus and negative for other respiratory viruses and atypical bacteria. Epstein-Barr virus DNA PCR was positive at 8696 copies/mL; tests for HIV, cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis A, B, and C were negative.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of hip pain following low-impact falls. Initial imaging revealed stress fractures of the left rib, left sacrum, and left femoral neck. Laboratory studies showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 220 U/L (reference range, 30–95), a phosphorus level of 2.1 mg/dL (2.5–5.0), creatinine 0.56 mg/dL, and 25-OH vitamin D 14.8 ng/mL (30–95). Outpatient evaluation demonstrated 1,25[OH]2D3 <8 pg/mL (18–72), calcium 9.3 mg/dL, albumin 4.28 g/dL, parathyroid hormone 37.9 pg/mL, ferritin 16.9 ng/mL, 24-hour urine phosphorus 0.5 g (0.3–1.3 g), urine creatinine 0.9 g/24 h (1–2 g/24 h), thyroid-stimulating hormone 2.54 mIU/L, and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) 1241 RU/mL (<180). Bone densitometry showed Z-scores of −2.5 in the lumbar spine and −1.9 in the femoral neck, and an octreotide scan was negative. She was treated with calcitriol and phosphate and underwent percutaneous pinning of the femoral neck. She became pregnant; her phosphate and calcitriol were adjusted to maintain normal phosphorus levels, and genetic evaluation for hypophosphatemic disorders, including X-linked hypophosphatemia, was unremarkable. Family history was negative for bone disease. After a planned cesarean delivery, she continued to have disabling bilateral hip, knee, and ankle pain. On re-presentation, examination revealed a slow gait with a limp and lumbar tenderness. Current labs on calcitriol 0.5 mcg daily and elemental phosphorus 500 mg twice daily included alkaline phosphatase 204 U/L, phosphorus 1.6 mg/dL, 25-OH vitamin D 32 ng/mL, 1,25[OH]2D3 32.4 pg/mL, calcium 9 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and parathyroid hormone 74 pg/mL. Phosphate supplementation was increased to three times daily, raising the phosphorus level to 2.3 mg/dL. A gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/MRI showed a 9×8-mm intracortical lesion in the anterolateral right fibular head (standard uptake value [SUV], 65), with additional uptake in a right femoral neck stress fracture (SUV, 5.6) and bilateral calcaneal stress fractures (SUV, 4).

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 57-year-old man with stage cS4a mantle cell lymphoma in complete remission after induction chemoimmunotherapy presented in August 2018 with painful swelling of the calves. There was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or soft-tissue infection. He reported a brief gastroenteritis episode at that time. Diuretics gave transient relief, but over weeks the swelling spread to the upper extremities and trunk muscles. Systemic steroids and a short discontinuation of ibrutinib had no effect.

By November 2018, calf swelling worsened; examination was notable only for one slightly enlarged right inguinal lymph node. Laboratory tests showed elevated LDH and CK, with negative autoimmune serology. Analgesics provided minimal benefit. In January 2019, CT scan showed no lymphoma relapse but diffuse subcutaneous edema. The patient’s condition deteriorated, and he was hospitalized with generalized muscle pain, ECOG performance status 3, massive edema (especially of the lower extremities), and extreme muscle tenderness. Neurologic exam showed only weak symmetric fist closure and shoulder lift; no focal deficits.

Initial evaluations were consistent with myositis of unknown cause. Ibrutinib and rituximab were discontinued. Laboratory testing revealed elevated CRP, transaminases, CK, troponin I, myoglobin, and LDH, with reduced plasma protein, albumin, and IgG; leukocyte count was elevated. MRI of the thighs showed diffuse intramuscular and extramuscular edema. Muscle biopsy demonstrated interstitial and perivascular T-cell and macrophage infiltrates with variation in fiber size, centrally located nuclei, necrosis, and regeneration. The patient developed acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Troponin I rose further; ECG revealed a new right bundle branch block and repolarization disturbances, and he developed atrial fibrillation. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocarditis. Over the next days, increasing somnolence and personality changes were noted. Brain MRI was unremarkable, but spinal MRI demonstrated a hyperintense lesion concerning for myelitis. CSF analysis showed leukocyte count 329/μl, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, and protein 79.6 mg/dl.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
An 82-year-old man with epithelioid pleural mesothelioma (cT1N0M0) was treated with ipilimumab and nivolumab. After eight courses, follow-up chest CT showed new bilateral infiltrative shadows. He reported fever and dyspnea. Laboratory tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein and surfactant protein D levels; Krebs von den Lungen-6 was normal. Sputum cultures, procalcitonin, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative. Serologic testing for anti–nuclear antigen, anti–aminoacyl–tRNA synthetase, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, anti-Sjögren’s-syndrome-related antigen A and B, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antigen antibodies were all negative. He had no history of antigen exposure. Immunotherapy was discontinued. He received lascufloxacin and then tazobactam/ceftolozane without improvement; oxygen requirement increased to 2 L/min. Based on the clinical picture and imaging, grade 3 ICI-induced pneumonitis was suspected. He underwent methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days followed by prednisolone 60 mg/day for 8 days, but chest radiographs remained unchanged and oxygen needs rose to 4 L/min. A second course of methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days produced no clinical improvement. One week later, bronchoscopy showed no airway secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 29% neutrophils, 58% lymphocytes, 13% macrophages, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.33. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy, and cultures of bronchoscopy specimens were negative. Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with steroid-refractory ICI-induced pneumonitis.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 44-year-old Hispanic woman presented with six months of progressive generalized weakness, a 40-pound weight loss over four months, and two weeks of dyspnea. She had a five-year history of hypertension treated with lisinopril but had been noncompliant for over three years. She denied alcohol, illicit drug use, and was a lifelong non-smoker.

On examination, she appeared ill and wasted, with mucosal pallor and non-tender, rubbery axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. There was no skin rash, joint deformities, or peripheral edema. The abdomen was mildly distended but non-tender, without organomegaly. Respiratory examination revealed dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the left lung base. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations were unremarkable.

Initial laboratory findings:
• Hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, hematocrit 20.9%, platelets 544 ×10^9/L  
• White blood cell count 3.5 ×10^9/L (neutrophils 80.4%, lymphocytes 16%)  
• Sodium 131 mM/L, potassium 5.7 mM/L, chloride 105 mM/L, bicarbonate 18 mM/L  
• Blood urea nitrogen 60 mg/dL, creatinine 1.69 mg/dL  
• Urinalysis: trace proteinuria  

Chest radiography showed bilateral pleural effusions; thoracentesis revealed an exudative effusion. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and an axillary lymph node biopsy were negative for malignancy. HIV and tuberculin skin testing were negative.

On hospital day 4, she developed acute inflammatory arthritis of the elbows and knees. Serologic tests revealed high titers of ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, and anti–Smith antibodies, with low complement C3 levels. Urinalysis showed pH 5, 16 WBCs and 27 RBCs per high-power field, and 24-hour urinary protein 0.81 g/day. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate was 53 mL/min/1.73 m^2, and leukopenia recurred on multiple occasions.

On day 5, she experienced worsening dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat chest radiography demonstrated reaccumulation of pleural effusions, and echocardiography showed a pericardial effusion. Arterial blood gas and concurrent basic metabolic panel revealed a non–anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia (pH 7.34, pCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3– 14 mM/L; Na 145 mM/L, K 5.5 mM/L, Cl 120 mM/L, HCO3– 19 mM/L, BUN 67 mg/dL, creatinine 1.09 mg/dL). Morning serum aldosterone was less than 1 ng/dL.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 64-year-old woman presented with a slowly enlarging mass in the left labia majora over 10 years. Her vital signs were normal. On examination, the mass was firm, painless, immobile, and measured approximately 7 × 4 cm, extending toward the mons pubis. Routine laboratory tests were normal. 

Surgical history:
– In 2000, a mass in the Bartholin’s gland was excised; histopathology in 2007 showed chondroid syringoma.  
– One year later, a recurrence in the labia majora was resected; histology showed clear cell hidradenoma (“lobular glandular proliferation of cuboid cells with no anaplasia”).  
– Most recently, ultrasound revealed a 4.2 × 8 cm heterogeneous, hypervascular subcutaneous mass; CT scan demonstrated a 3.8 × 7.2 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing lesion in the left labia majora extending to the anterior perineum, and a low-density focus in the liver suggestive of a simple cyst.  
– The vulvar mass was excised; on gross examination it measured 7 × 3 × 4 cm, was gray and well-circumscribed, and was reported again as chondroid syringoma.  

Three months later, the patient noted another recurrence near the fourchette. The lesion was excised and submitted for histopathologic evaluation.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
An 8‐year‐old boy with no significant past medical history presented with a 30-minute history of generalized abdominal pain followed by a single episode of vomiting. During the event he developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact, without loss of consciousness, abnormal movements, or sphincter relaxation. The episode lasted 10 minutes, after which he reported a frontal headache (5/10) and persistent nausea. Family denied toxin or medication exposure. He had a similar episode 18 months earlier, diagnosed as migraine. There was no personal or family history of epilepsy or neurological disorders. Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate, and he was performing well in school.

On admission, his vital signs were normal except for blood pressure above the 95th percentile for age. Neurologic examination revealed confusion and disorientation; he could not recognize his mother or speak but could follow visual commands. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Approximately 20 minutes after arrival, his consciousness and orientation improved. Over the next hours he had three additional self‐limited vomiting episodes and ongoing headache, which improved after a single IV dose of diclofenac (1 mg/kg).

Complete blood count, serum chemistries, and electrolytes (including sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus) were all within normal limits. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol was reported as normal for age.

A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 74-year-old right-handed woman was brought to the psychiatry clinic with a 5-month history of abrupt onset of disorganized speech, severe anxiety, and self-harm behaviors that began after a family trip. Her speech was rapid, fluent, and nonsensical—exemplified by the phrase “Our neighbor has gone to the cobbler to buy Ghormeh Sabzi”—consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. Over the ensuing months, she developed agitation, persecutory delusions, visual and auditory hallucinations, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a persistent urge to flee her home.

Her psychiatric history included a 10-year history of depression treated with sertraline. There was no prior cognitive impairment or neurological disease. On examination, she was disoriented to time, demonstrated anomia, and had marked perseveration on the Clock Drawing Test, impaired performance on Luria’s three-step test, and defective crossed-pentagon drawing. Cognitive testing revealed an MMSE score of 2/30 and an ACE-R score of 2/100, likely confounded by comprehension deficits.

An initial brain MRI performed 2 months after symptom onset was reported as normal. She was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and started on memantine and quetiapine, without clinical improvement. Because of the acute presentation and prominent frontal and temporal features, she was referred to neurology for further assessment.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 48‐year‐old woman with a history of asthma presented with a 2‐day history of right lower‐extremity numbness and pain that worsened despite conservative measures. She denied any low back pain. On examination, manual muscle testing of the right tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus was 3/5, and gastrocnemius and flexor hallucis longus were 4/5; deep‐tendon reflexes were normal. Straight‐leg‐raising was positive at 70 degrees; the femoral‐nerve stretch test was negative. 

Plain radiographs showed degenerative scoliosis at L5–S1. Lumbar MRI demonstrated a right‐sided disc herniation at L5–S1 without significant nerve‐root or cord compression. Initial peroneal‐nerve conduction studies revealed a motor conduction velocity of 51.5 m/s. Ankle‐brachial indices were decreased (0.78 on the right, 0.73 on the left), but lower‐extremity arteriography showed no significant vascular lesions. Based on these findings, she was diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation and treated symptomatically with Neurotropin®. 

By day 7, muscle strength nearly normalized, but lateral leg pain persisted. On day 22, pain increased, and by day 26 she developed right foot drop (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, flexor hallucis longus, and peroneus longus 1/5; left side 4/5) with absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally. Urgent MRI showed no new nerve‐root compression. Repeat peroneal conduction studies failed to elicit an evoked myogenic potential. On day 30, she was unable to walk and was admitted for further evaluation.

A 63-year-old woman was admitted with insidious upper abdominal pain unrelated to food ingestion and nausea, and after an episode of intense acute abdominal pain. She denied hematemesis or melena. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, homogeneous, oval mass arising from the posterior gastric wall, measuring approximately 10×6×11 cm, compressing the second portion of the duodenum; the lesion had fat-tissue attenuation with central contrast enhancement and trabecular architecture but did not invade the peripheral layers.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 62-year-old man presented with a two-week history of an asymptomatic swelling in the right lower half of the face and reduced mouth opening. He reported two prior similar episodes over eight years: the first, five years ago, was treated as a buccal-space infection with incision and drainage; the second, two years ago, resolved spontaneously. He had no pain or fever and was a known diabetic on regular medication. 

On examination, there was gross right facial asymmetry. Extraorally, a 6 × 6 cm ovoid subcutaneous swelling extended from the level of the right lateral canthus to 1 cm below the corner of the mouth and from the corner of the mouth posteriorly to the mandibular ramus. The borders were ill-defined, the consistency ranged from soft to firm, and the overlying skin was normal. There was no lymphadenopathy, paresthesia, or facial palsy. Intraorally, the right buccal mucosa was elevated and glistening, with no vestibular obliteration; mouth opening was restricted by the mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the face showed a well-defined soft-tissue mass with cystic areas in the right buccal space. Intracystic loculations with dense cystic content were noted, and there was erosion of the posterior buccal cortex without perforation of the maxilla; the maxillary antrum was compressed.

A clinical diagnosis of a nonspecific chronic abscess with buccal-space involvement was made. Under general anesthesia, an intraoral approach was used to excise the lesion in toto with a margin of fibrous tissue. The lesion shelled out easily, with no involvement of buccinator muscle or bone. The excised specimen measured 4.8 × 4.5 cm, was creamish-brown, firm, irregular, and had a leathery pouch-like appearance, entirely within the soft tissue of the buccal space.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 41-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 2-year history of progressively worsening fever, weight loss, night sweats, and a dry cough. He also reported chronic lower back pain without neurologic deficits and a painful nonhealing ulcer on his right hallux. He had two sputum GeneXpert tests at local clinics, both negative. He was treated symptomatically with paracetamol, NSAIDs, and topical antibacterials.  

On referral for the toe ulcer, examination revealed a cachectic man who was normotensive and afebrile, with no lymphadenopathy or edema. He had tenderness over the thoracic spine but no neurologic deficits. Laboratory tests showed:  
• Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, white cells 7.3×10^9/L, platelets 369×10^9/L  
• ESR >130 mm/hr, CRP 113 mg/L  
• IgA 6.2 g/L, anti-DNase B 259 IU/mL  
• Negative ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis serologies  
• Urine protein-creatinine ratio 0.242 g/mmol; dipstick: 3+ leukocytes, 3+ red blood cells; microscopy: granular casts; urine culture: no growth  

Chest radiograph showed bilateral reticular-nodular opacities. An induced sputum was trace positive for MTB on GeneXpert and subsequently grew MTB sensitive to rifampicin and isoniazid. Biopsy of the toe ulcer showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with a solitary acid-fast bacillus. MRI of the spine revealed contiguous spondylitis from T6 to T10 with discitis and an epidural/paraspinal collection causing spinal cord compression. Renal ultrasound demonstrated normal-sized kidneys with increased echogenicity.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 69-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of a painless, firm area of induration and mild erythema below her left lower eyelid. Her history included chronic scleritis treated successfully with NSAIDs, left levator resection for ptosis, and a dacryocystorhinostomy one month before the onset of the lesion. The mass persisted despite two courses of antibiotics for presumed postoperative cellulitis. Three months after surgery, the nodule remained stable in size. 

On examination, there was a focal, non-tender, indurated elevation along the inferior orbital rim. A CT scan of the orbits demonstrated soft-tissue thickening of the anterior-inferior orbital rim and lower eyelid without extension into surrounding structures or bony invasion. 

An excisional biopsy was performed. Intraoperative frozen sections revealed granulomatous inflammation. The final histopathology showed granulomatous inflammation with central necrobiosis, extensive Alcian-Blue positive mucin, and scattered multinucleated giant cells. There was no evidence of malignancy, and bacterial and fungal stains (Ziehl–Neelsen and Grocott) were negative.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 42-year-old man presented with a 1.5-year history of abdominal pain and three loose, watery stools daily. He had gastroesophageal reflux disease and hereditary hemochromatosis (grade 3 iron overload, mild portal fibrosis, C282Y homozygosity). He denied rectal bleeding, fever, or weight loss. Vital signs were normal, and physical examination was unremarkable. 
 
Laboratory evaluation showed negative ova and parasites, bacterial culture, fecal leukocytes, and Clostridium difficile NAAT. Histoplasma antigen, anti-transglutaminase, and anti-endomysial antibodies were negative. Rapid plasma reagin and Tropheryma whipplei testing were also negative. 
 
Colonoscopy revealed erythematous mucosa in the transverse colon and rectum and congestion in the terminal ileum. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed diffuse gastric erythema with erosions and duodenitis. Biopsies from the stomach, duodenum, terminal ileum, colon, and rectum all demonstrated non-caseating microgranulomas; acid-fast bacilli and fungal stains were negative, and no Helicobacter pylori organisms were identified. 
 
CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed hepatosplenomegaly; a prior liver biopsy showed no granulomas. Chest CT was unremarkable. Angiotensin-converting enzyme level was elevated at 77 U/L.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 68-year-old man with pseudophakic bullous keratopathy underwent Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK) in the right eye. His postoperative course was initially uneventful under topical and systemic corticosteroids. He had a history of an eye infection by Thaumetopoea pityocampa (pine processionary) 9 months before DSAEK, which had resolved prior to surgery.

Two months after DSAEK, he was referred for evaluation of keratitis in the right eye. On examination:
• Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye.  
• Pupils were isocoric and isoreactive without an afferent pupillary defect.  
• There was no pain with ocular movements.  
• Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye showed brown, multilobular lesions confined to the deep corneal stroma, with no conjunctival hyperemia, no discharge, and no epithelial defect.  
• The anterior chamber was deep and clear. Intraocular pressure and fundus examination were normal. The left eye was unremarkable.

Anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the right eye revealed a central infiltrate involving all corneal layers and a peripheral infiltrate concentrated in the deep stroma.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

strict_queue_context.vignette:
An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He also reported anorexia and a 12% body-weight loss over six months.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). Cardiac and chest examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was normal. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in left hip and knee flexors and extensors; the rest of the exam was normal.  
Initial laboratory results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 76 mg/L, WCC 11.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 × 10^9/L) and pre-renal acute-on-chronic kidney injury.  
An initial differential of cauda equina syndrome or epidural abscess prompted an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine, which showed mild foraminal narrowing at L5–S1 but no central canal stenosis or abscess. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture.  
Despite analgesia, his left hip pain worsened, strength declined to 2/5 at the hip and 3/5 at the knee, and CRP and ESR continued to rise. A left hip ultrasound revealed a small anterior joint effusion. Normal tumour markers, MRI of the hip, and an isotope bone scan argued against malignancy. Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted.  
An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 60-year-old man with a history of heavy cigarette smoking, emphysema, hypertension, and prostate cancer in remission presented with a 4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. On admission, he was febrile (38.5°C), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min); examination revealed peritonism in the right lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding, innumerable hepatic nodules, mural thickening of the cecum and sigmoid colon, and marked mesenteric, para-aortic, and portocaval lymphadenopathy; there was also pulmonary consolidation and collapse in the right lower lobe. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a perforated appendix with four-quadrant purulent contamination and a thickened, woody sigmoid colon; a subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy was performed. Postoperatively, he remained ventilated. On day 2, CT of the chest for staging demonstrated bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi. An extubation attempt on day 3 failed, and the patient died on day 6 after withdrawal of care.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 14-year-old girl presented with 6 months of discomfort at the tip of the left middle finger. She had noted that the finger was larger than the others since birth and that it grew progressively. Three months before presentation, she developed tingling at the fingertip and limited flexion of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, the middle finger was enlarged but the overlying skin was normal. There was tenderness throughout the enlargement, the temperature was normal, and sensation was decreased distally. Resistance to flexion prevented full finger flexion. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. A CT scan of the hand showed overgrowth of the proximal, middle, and distal phalanges plus surrounding soft tissue; normal bone trabeculation; and no abnormal vascular structures, suggesting a lipomatous process.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 21-year-old woman with autism spectrum disorder (on risperidone) and intellectual disability was brought to the hospital after a witnessed collapse. She had no prior history of syncope, cardiac arrest, or known cardiovascular disease, and her family denied any illicit drug or alcohol use. strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 59-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a crusty lesion in the right fronto-orbital region present for several months. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was an irregularly shaped 5 × 3 cm plaque with multiple superficial crusts. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 

An excisional biopsy of the lesion showed lobules and detached aggregates of eosinophilic keratinocytes with pleomorphic nuclei and prominent nucleoli infiltrating the reticular dermis; there was no clear evidence of basaloid nests, and the diagnosis rendered was invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. 

On April 24, he began treatment with cemiplimab 350 mg every 3 weeks. Before therapy, ^18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a focal area of uptake in the supraorbital lesion (SUVmax 6.9; metabolic tumor volume, 2 cc). After five cycles, the plaque had regressed markedly, but several discrete papular lesions remained. Dermoscopic evaluation of these papules revealed features typical of basal cell carcinoma. A follow-up PET/CT at 12 weeks showed decreased uptake in the original lesion (SUVmax 4.8; metabolic tumor volume, 0.5 cc), consistent with partial metabolic response.

A 35-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of radicular pain radiating from her lower back down the left leg, with occasional tingling. Electromyography showed neuropathic irritation of the left L4, L5, S1, and S2 roots, most severe at L5, with no denervation. Lumbosacral gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed a solitary, completely cystic mass in the left L5–S1 foraminal zone extending along the course of the sciatic nerve into the left ischial groove, measuring approximately 13.9 cm in length and 1.9 cm in maximal diameter. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated peripheral rim enhancement, causing severe foraminal stenosis without attachment to pelvic organs. MR neurography confirmed that the mass arose from the sciatic nerve at the left ischial groove.

A 55-year-old man underwent right hemicolectomy for moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon, staged as IIIB (T4N1M0). He had no thrombophilic disorders. Preoperative carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and CA19-9 levels were normal. He completed six months of adjuvant chemotherapy. CTAP showed absence of the right portal vein and a perfusion defect throughout the right lobe, suggestive of portal vein tumor thrombus.  
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography showed no communication with the biliary tree, and bile cytology was negative for malignancy.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 64-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, chills, or fever. She had no history of hepatitis, surgery, or hereditary disease, and no underlying medical conditions. On examination, she was afebrile and oriented; there was right upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or palpable masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, and negative Murphy’s sign and shifting dullness.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• AFP 2.4 µg/l (normal 0.0–7.0)  
• CEA 11.6 µg/l (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• CA-125 32.3 KIU/l (normal 0.0–35.0)  
• CA19-9 228.0 KIU/l (normal 0.0–30.0)  
• Other liver enzymes and blood counts largely within reference ranges, except WBC 11.9×10^9/l (normal 3.5–9.5×10^9/l).

Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous echoic mass near the gallbladder fossa in the right liver lobe, calcifications in the right liver, multiple gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening, and enhanced pancreatic echogenicity. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a lesion in the right hepatic lobe adjacent to the gallbladder fossa, multiple enlarged hepatic hilar lymph nodes, and findings of gallstones with cholecystitis. Liver MRI demonstrated an occupying lesion in the right lobe with mild intrahepatic bile duct dilatation, raising the possibility of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, along with gallstones and cholecystitis. No extrahepatic primary tumor was identified.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 2-month-old full-term female with known complex congenital heart disease (single ventricle defect, double-outlet right ventricle with D-transposition of the great arteries, and an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with left superior vena cava) was admitted for evaluation of occasional cyanosis. She was in good general condition, weighed 5 kg, had an oxygen saturation of 80%, and showed no signs of respiratory distress. Her medications included furosemide and spironolactone. The team planned a pulmonary artery banding, but during the procedure the patient became hemodynamically unstable and suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest requiring cardiac massage, so the operation was aborted. To gather hemodynamic data, cardiac catheterization was performed via the left femoral artery, with the catheter tip in the single ventricle, using serial doses of nonionic iodinated contrast (Iopromide) totaling 3 mL/kg over 30 minutes. Approximately 12 hours after the procedure, the patient developed clonic movements of the left upper limb and persistent sucking motions. A noncontrast head CT obtained after this first seizure showed a slight diffuse increase in cortical density predominantly in the right frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes and, to a lesser extent, in the left parietal and occipital lobes; there was no mass effect, hemorrhage, or other intracranial abnormality.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 38-year-old woman presented with 4 months of progressively worsening symmetric pain in the small joints of her hands, wrists, knees, and ankles. She reported early morning stiffness lasting 2 hours daily and severe fatigue throughout the day. One month before presentation, she had a mild COVID-19 infection confirmed by SARS-CoV-2 PCR; symptoms were limited to fever, chills, and a non-oxygen-requiring cough. She had not been vaccinated against COVID-19 at that time. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, rash, or appetite changes since recovering. There were no recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections and no history of psoriasis or uveitis. She is a non-smoker, does not drink alcohol, and has no recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 13 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein of 4.3 mg/L (both within normal limits). Immunologic testing revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:640, negative extractable nuclear antigen and double-stranded DNA antibodies, a rheumatoid factor of 62.29 IU/mL (normal <20 IU/mL), and an anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody of 237.39 units (normal <20 units). Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Radiographs of the hands, knees, ankles, and feet were unremarkable. Hand ultrasound showed no joint erosion. MRI of the hands demonstrated synovitis of the bilateral distal radioulnar joints and the left second metacarpophalangeal joint, with tenosynovitis around the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon; no osseous destruction was identified.

- MUC6: positive throughout the region.
- Chromogranin A: slight enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia.

- Anti-parietal cell antibody: <1:10 (negative)
- Anti-intrinsic factor antibody: negative
- Serum gastrin: 150 pg/mL (normal 37–172)
- Vitamin B12: 870 pg/mL (normal 233–914)
- Anti-H. pylori IgG: <3 U/mL (negative)

A 38-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of hypertension first noted at age 24 during pregnancy and again at age 38 after a basal ganglia hemorrhage. - Normochromic microcytic anemia and thrombocytopenia on full blood examination; other laboratory tests, including thyroid function, cortisol, aldosterone–renin ratio, urinary metanephrines, and renal function, were unremarkable.  
- Lipid profile showed low HDL and elevated triglycerides.  
- Renal Doppler ultrasound excluded renal artery stenosis but revealed incidental bilateral adrenal lesions and hepatosplenomegaly.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed bilateral adrenal lesions (32 HU noncontrast; absolute washout 76.5%, relative washout 39%) that were unchanged after 8 months, and gross hepatosplenomegaly with dilated portal and splenic veins.  
She had no symptoms of adrenal hormone excess, and her blood pressure was controlled on a single antihypertensive agent.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A male newborn was referred at 1 day of age for cyanosis; oxygen saturation (SaO2) was 80% in room air. Laboratory findings showed a hematocrit of 47.8% and a platelet count of 103 000/mm3; other values were normal and there were no signs of infection. Echocardiography revealed pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus. A prostaglandin infusion was started, raising SaO2 to 90–95%. On day 11, he underwent a systemic‐to‐pulmonary shunt operation with graft placement and PDA division. Preoperative values on day 10 were hematocrit 38.9%, platelet count 173 000/mm3, and SaO2 95% on prostaglandin. Postoperatively, hematocrit was 52.1% and platelet count was 58 000/mm3; platelet count then increased without transfusion. By postoperative day 6, he was extubated with SaO2 80–85%, hematocrit 41.1%, and platelet count 123 000/mm3. He was discharged on postoperative day 13 with SaO2 85–87%, hematocrit 33.4%, and platelet count 225 000/mm3.

At 10 months of age, he was admitted for a Rastelli operation. His SaO2 was 80%; hematocrit was 49.1% and platelet count was 68 000/mm3. He had no bleeding history or medications. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and INR were normal; peripheral smear was unremarkable. Antiplatelet antibodies and platelet‐associated immunoglobulins were negative; antinuclear and anti–double‐stranded DNA antibodies were normal. Platelet aggregation time was 127 s (reference, 61–110 s). Viral and bacterial studies were insignificant. The pediatrician made a provisional diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia and administered intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg) the day before surgery. On the day of operation, hematocrit was 42.6% and platelet count was 77 000/mm3.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 36‐year‐old man of Indian origin presented at 2:30 a.m. with acute right‐sided weakness and three episodes of vomiting. He awoke around midnight with headache and vomiting, then noted right‐sided numbness and weakness; there was no visual change or speech disturbance. He had experienced odd sensations and occasional tremors in his right arm and leg over the prior two weeks but had not sought care. His medical history was unremarkable. He was a nonsmoker, denied alcohol or drug use, and worked as a teacher. 

On examination, pulse was 88 bpm, blood pressure 124/87 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) with intact speech. Findings included partial left ptosis, bilateral torsional nystagmus on vertical and horizontal gaze, equal reactive pupils, and no ophthalmoplegia. Motor strength was 0/5 in the right upper limb, 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the right lower limb; left‐sided strength was normal. Reflexes were brisk bilaterally with right ankle clonus; the right plantar response was upgoing. Sensation was intact. NIH Stroke Scale score was 7. Cardiorespiratory examination was normal.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology but revealed an incidental 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma. CT angiography demonstrated normal opacification of cervical and intracranial arteries; CT perfusion was symmetric. Admission laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, and kidney, liver, and thyroid function tests, were normal except for a total protein of 87 g/L (normal 60–80). Chest radiograph and 12‐lead ECG were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study was unremarkable. HbA1c was 5.4%; lipid profile was within normal limits. 

Brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla without hemorrhagic transformation; the small frontal cavernoma was again noted. MR angiography was unremarkable. A diagnosis of ischemic stroke in a 36‐year‐old gentleman with no apparent risk factors was made, and further investigations were initiated to look for the cause.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 61-year-old African American woman with bilateral knee osteoarthritis presented three days after her third weekly Synvisc viscosupplementation injections in each knee with acute bilateral knee swelling and pain, left greater than right. She reported onset of pain 12 hours after the injections and denied fever, chills, or malaise. On examination, her right knee had a suprapatellar effusion, range of motion 0–70°, no erythema, and no pain with micromotion. Her left knee had a moderate suprapatellar effusion, range of motion 0–30°, no erythema, and pain with micromotion. Laboratory testing showed a peripheral white blood cell count of 12.8×10^3/mm³, a C-reactive protein level of 159 mg/L, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 79 mm/hr. Bilateral knee arthrocentesis yielded the following synovial fluid results: Left knee, 38,580 WBC/mm³, negative gram stain, negative cultures; Right knee, 29,670 WBC/mm³, negative gram stain, negative cultures.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 67‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of a painless right vulvar mass extending into the right inguinal region. She first noted the lesion two years earlier, with gradual enlargement over the past four months. She denied pain, changes in appetite or bowel habits, urinary symptoms, weight loss, infection, or bleeding. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, managed with valsartan/amlodipine, and a hysterectomy in 2016 for abnormal uterine bleeding. She was post‐menopausal, had no history of hormone therapy, and did not smoke or drink alcohol.

On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. Inspection revealed a 12 cm, non‐tender mass of the right labia majora extending to the right groin, without erythema, lymphadenopathy, or signs of inflammation. Pelvic exam was otherwise normal.

Soft‐tissue ultrasound showed a well‐defined, hypoechoic solid mass measuring 90 × 44 × 55 mm in the right labia majora tracking into the inguinal canal, with mild peripheral blood flow on Doppler imaging. Routine laboratory results, including blood counts and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. The leading preoperative impression was a canal of Nuck hernia containing omental tissue.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 47-year-old Caucasian woman with a 23-year history of presumed multiple sclerosis—characterized by four episodes of optic neuritis since 1989, a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis in 1995, persistently negative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) oligoclonal bands, and unremarkable brain MRI scans—was treated with monthly intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and interferon-β. In January 2012, she presented with subacute onset of expressive aphasia and right-sided hemiparesis. On examination, she was alert with expressive language impairment and 3/5 strength in the right arm and leg; vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies demonstrated a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. Brain MRI showed a large T2-hyperintense, tumefactive lesion in the left prefrontal white matter and smaller T2 lesions on the right without clear evidence of a disturbed blood–brain barrier. MR spectroscopy revealed an unchanged choline peak. CSF analysis was unremarkable, with no evidence of intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, no oligoclonal bands, and a normal cell count. Time-of-flight MR angiography showed no signs of vasculitis, and laboratory work-up revealed no clinical or serological evidence for connective tissue diseases. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody titre was 1:1000 by cell-based assay.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 17-year-old single Turkish woman presented with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, and right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. She had no known exposure to tuberculosis. On examination she was afebrile with tender right lower abdominal quadrant and no rebound. Initial abdominal and chest radiographs were normal, and a bedside abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,200/μL, C-reactive protein of 12 mg/L, blood urea nitrogen of 35 mg/dL, and creatinine of 1.02 mg/dL. Urinalysis was unremarkable and a urine human chorionic gonadotropin test was negative. HIV testing was negative. While under observation, a second abdominopelvic ultrasound was interpreted as suggestive of retrocecal appendicitis. The patient was taken to the operating room via a McBurney’s incision. A 15 × 6 cm cystic mass with regular margins was found arising from the right tubo-ovarian complex; the appendix appeared clinically normal. The mass was excised intact, the tubo-ovarian structures were preserved, and on incision of the cyst wall purulent fluid was noted. Cultures were deferred until after the weekend.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 61-year-old woman with type II diabetes presented with several days of urinary retention and inability to ambulate in the setting of a 1-year history of progressive lower-extremity weakness and a 100-lb unintentional weight loss. Her weakness began in the proximal left leg, gradually involved the right leg and both hands, and was accompanied by worsening numbness and tingling in her feet; she became wheelchair-dependent within 6 months. She denied pain, flank pain, hematuria, fevers, visual changes, speech or swallowing difficulty. On examination, she was alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II–XII were intact. She had bilateral weakness of hip flexors, knee flexors, knee extensors, and intrinsic hand muscles, with atrophy of the hands and thighs. Sensation to light touch was reduced in the feet, with slight impairment of vibration and proprioception. Reflexes were 2+ in the upper extremities and absent at the knees and ankles; plantar responses were flexor. Bladder catheterization yielded 1.8 L of retained urine. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count; sodium 117 mmol/L; chloride 87 mmol/L; blood urea nitrogen 0.89 mg/dL; creatinine 25 mg/dL. Urine was negative for protein or bacteria. CSF analysis revealed protein 175 mg/dL, glucose 105 mg/dL, 1 WBC, 0 RBC; CSF cytology was negative for malignancy. Lyme serology, autoimmune panel, and a comprehensive paraneoplastic antibody panel were negative. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.5 g/dL. On hospital day 4, electromyography and nerve conduction studies demonstrated decreased amplitudes in motor and sensory nerves, slowed conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, and absent sensory responses, suggesting a chronic length-dependent sensorimotor demyelinating polyneuropathy with superimposed chronic lumbosacral plexopathy. MRI of the pelvis showed bilateral femoral nerve enlargement without enhancement.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 67-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, active smoking (35 pack-years), a family history of ischaemic heart disease, and prior percutaneous coronary interventions (2008, 2017, 2022) for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction presented with Canadian Cardiovascular Society Class III angina. A recent exercise stress test induced angina at 50 W without ECG changes. On admission, he appeared anxious; the physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, Q waves in lead III, and biphasic T waves in leads III and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65% without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated patent stents in the circumflex artery, non-significant disease in the left anterior descending artery, and significant ostial right coronary artery stenosis with in-stent restenosis in the mid-segment, which was treated with three drug-eluting stents. After transfer to the intensive care unit, he complained of worsening chest pain; ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V3, and echocardiography remained normal. A second angiogram showed patent stents but subocclusion of the right coronary postero-lateral branch, successfully treated with balloon angioplasty, relieving his pain. Shortly thereafter, he developed recurrent sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation requiring seven external shocks and 15 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Post-resuscitation ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with persistent precordial ST-segment elevation and new QTc prolongation to 500 ms. Repeat echocardiography revealed akinesia of all apical segments, later extending to mid-segments, hyperkinesia of the basal segments, and severely reduced LVEF of 35%, leading to suspicion of takotsubo syndrome.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 27-year-old man with a history of a 5 mm‐thick melanoma on his posterior neck treated six years earlier by wide local excision (no sentinel lymph node biopsy, no adjuvant therapy) presented with hemoptysis and dyspnea. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable only for scattered breath sounds without stridor. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 3.1 × 2.7 × 3.6 cm mass in the right lower lobe. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the lung lesion demonstrated a malignant small round blue cell tumor. Molecular studies were negative for an EWSR1 translocation but otherwise were interpreted as consistent with Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET). 

Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT showed an FDG-avid right lower lobe mass and an intensely FDG-avid, partially calcified 4.1 × 2.3 × 2.8 cm expansile lesion within the right hyoid bone. Ultrasound–guided core needle biopsy of the hyoid lesion was nondiagnostic, yielding only rare atypical epithelial cells amidst lymphocytes.

A multidisciplinary sarcoma tumor board concluded that the hyoid lesion most likely represented a synchronous primary bone tumor (e.g., plasmacytoma, chondrosarcoma, or osteosarcoma). Given his pulmonary symptoms and the potential for chemotherapy to treat both lesions, he received 14 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide (VCD/IE). 

Mid-treatment PET/CT demonstrated a substantial decrease in size and complete metabolic response of the lung mass but development of right neck adenopathy and interval growth of the hyoid bone lesion, suggesting a distinct pathology.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 54-year-old man with glioblastoma treated by surgical resection began a clinical trial with M7824 (a bifunctional fusion protein targeting PD-L1 and TGF-β). Four weeks after initiation of M7824, he presented with a severely pruritic, nontender, erythematous papular and macular eruption on his back, bilateral ankles, and upper extremities. He was not receiving any other new medications. The oncology team initially classified the eruption as a grade I rash and prescribed hydrocortisone 1% cream and oral diphenhydramine, but the rash and pruritus progressed. One month later, the rash reached grade II severity, and doxycycline was started for a suspected acneiform eruption. On dermatologic evaluation, the consensus was that the eruption represented a drug reaction to M7824. Laboratory evaluation showed no elevations in liver enzymes, no eosinophilia, and no lymphadenopathy. The patient was treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment and hydroxyzine, but over the following two weeks the rash progressed to grade III with worsening pruritus. M7824 infusions were held, and prednisone at 40 mg per day was initiated according to guidelines, but his symptoms failed to improve.

A 6‐year‐old girl with no relevant medical history presented with intensely pruritic skin lesions on her anterior thighs. strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 40-year-old man presented with a painful nodule on the lower part of his right leg. He reported that the lesion had been stable in size and painless for 4 years but had enlarged and become tender over the past 6 months. There was no history of trauma or personal or family history of malignancy.

On examination, an irregular, firm, erythematous, mobile, tender mass measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm was noted just above the lateral malleolus of the right leg. No popliteal or inguinal lymphadenopathy was present, and there were no other suspicious cutaneous lesions. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, fasting blood sugar, liver and renal function tests, were within normal limits. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and HIV were negative.

The patient underwent a local excision. Grossly, there was a lobulated, tan-gray, firm mass partly covered by skin, measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm. On light microscopy, the dermal tumor extended into the superficial subcutis and was composed of nests and fascicles of spindle-shaped to epithelioid cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli within a collagenous stroma. Mitotic figures, including atypical forms, measured 7–8 per 10 high-power fields. There was no intracytoplasmic melanin pigment, and the overlying epidermis showed no increase in basal melanocytes, junctional activity, or pagetoid spread.

Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for vimentin and focal positivity for Melan-A and HMB-45. The tumor cells were negative for S-100 protein, pancytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, and CD31.

An 8-year-old, previously healthy, fully immunized girl presented with 5 days of intermittent fever followed by abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had been at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic; her parents had mild upper respiratory symptoms for 1 week. Outpatient oral antibiotics and IV fluids did not improve her symptoms. She was admitted to surgery with suspected appendicitis; abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Persistent fever, abdominal pain, and the emergence of a rash and conjunctivitis prompted transfer to the pediatric COVID-19 ward. 

On examination, temperature was 38.6 °C. She had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, erythematous throat, palmar erythema, a strawberry tongue, and an erythema multiforme–type rash; there was no hypotension, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI murmur at the left sternal border; lung sounds were normal.

Laboratory tests showed ESR 67 mm/h, CRP 166 mg/L, platelet count 192×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and WBC 10.3×10^9/L with 82% neutrophils. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 25-year-old Hispanic woman of African descent, previously healthy and a non-smoker, presented with a 1-month history of dyspnea on exertion, intermittent dry cough, hyporexia, and unquantified intermittent fever. She delayed care until an acute worsening of dyspnea led to emergency department evaluation, where she developed acute respiratory failure and pulseless electrical activity arrest. After orotracheal intubation and stabilization, she was transferred to our institution.

On arrival, she was sedated on mechanical ventilation. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 200/140 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 bpm, temperature 36 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed anisocoria (right pupil 5 mm, left 3 mm), jugular venous distension, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral coarse rales; no skin lesions or peripheral edema were present.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right paratracheal mediastinal mass compressing and displacing the trachea to the left, with adjacent right upper-lobe infiltrates. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and neck demonstrated an 11 × 8.6 × 9.5 cm lobulated solid mass arising from the right thoracic operculum/pleura, with a nodular pleural component, mass effect on the right hilum, supra-aortic vessels, and superior vena cava, pneumomediastinum, left pneumothorax, and lytic destruction with cortical fracture of the T1 and T2 vertebrae. Centrilobular opacities in the left upper lobe suggested aspiration pneumonitis.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 13.47 × 10^3/µL (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 303 × 10^3/µL, INR 1.39, lactic acid 2.83 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 4.20 mg/dL, LDH 592 U/L, calcium 6.58 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.73 mg/dL; arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.30, PCO2 44.5 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3 22.3 mmol/L, BE –3.7 mmol/L, and SO2 98%. She received dexamethasone and piperacillin/tazobactam. Given the atypical imaging features and concern for possible hematologic malignancy, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy was planned to obtain adequate tissue.

There was no personal or family history of cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease. Vital signs were: pulse 110/min, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37 °C, oxygen saturation 95% on room air (99% on 2 L/min nasal cannula). Cardiac auscultation was normal, and neck veins were not distended. Initial ECG showed sinus rhythm with 2 mm of ST-segment elevation in leads V2 and V3. She was given aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous heparin and taken to the catheterization laboratory. Twenty minutes later, a second ECG showed a new right bundle branch block and resolution of the precordial ST-segment elevations. Forty-five minutes after presentation, coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries without stenosis. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated right ventricular dilatation and an estimated pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated. 

On day 8, she developed febrile neutropenia and received piperacillin–tazobactam. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species grew in blood cultures, prompting addition of teicoplanin. Persistent fever led to repeat cultures, which grew Enterococcus species, and teicoplanin was replaced with daptomycin. High-resolution chest CT showed nonspecific nodules under 1 cm, and serum galactomannan antigen was negative. After 10 days of fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 20/μL, she reported severe pain in her right arm radiating to her shoulder, suggesting herpes zoster; however, no vesicles were present. On examination, there was a very tender point in the upper lateral scapular region with an underlying vague mass. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a focal cystic necrotic lesion between the teres minor and teres major muscles.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A female infant was born at 35 weeks 4 days’ gestation, weighing 2152 g. She was one of monochorionic diamniotic twins; her identical twin died in utero at 24 weeks. Fetal ultrasound had shown microcephaly and ventricular enlargement. Postnatal MRI of the head revealed microcephaly, marked enlargement of both lateral ventricles without signs of elevated intracranial pressure, and severe thinning of the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes; the temporal lobes, basal ganglia, thalamus, brain stem, and cerebellum were preserved. No intracranial hematoma or neoplastic lesions were seen. Family history was noncontributory. 

At 1 week of age, examination of the eyes showed very weak light reflexes bilaterally. The anterior chambers were slightly shallow, but there were no pupillary abnormalities, cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, or ptosis. Funduscopic examination revealed mild optic nerve pallor with suspected peripapillary double-ring sign. The fundus had a faint reddish tone; retinal vessels appeared normal in caliber and reached the periphery. No chorioretinal dysplasia was noted.

strict_queue_context.vignette:
A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by early satiety and urinary urgency. She denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and her mother had a history of ovarian cysts. On examination, the abdomen was distended with dull percussion notes but without tenderness or guarding.

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a cyst measuring 16 × 24 cm that compressed adjacent abdominal organs. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a large midline intraperitoneal cyst, 30 × 25.6 × 16.8 cm in size, extending from the liver to the pelvis and involving the uterus and ovaries. The lesion had a fluid density of 20 Hounsfield units and demonstrated no calcifications, soft-tissue components, or enhancing septations, suggesting a benign etiology.

Laboratory studies, including α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and cancer antigen 125, were all within normal limits; the Risk of Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) score was 4.1 %. Serological testing for Echinococcus granulosus was negative. A giant intra-abdominal cyst was diagnosed preoperatively, and laparoscopic cyst aspiration with exploration under general anesthesia was planned.
